Habibi Kebs has affordable doner kebabs in Kembangan
Doner kebabs are low-key an underrated option for a fast and affordable meal : they’re quick to prepare, portable, and packed full of vegetables for your daily dose of vitamins. So, next time you’re in Kembangan running errands or passing by on your daily jog along the park connectors, check out Habibi Kebs , a Muslim-owned eatery serving Berlin-inspired doner kebabs at nett prices.
Food at Habibi Kebs
For the uninitiated: doner kebabs are a traditional Turkish dish. The word “doner” comes from the Turkish term “dönmek”, meaning to “turn” or “rotate”, which aptly describes how it’s cooked: seasoned meat, usually chicken, beef, or lamb, is stacked on a vertical rotisserie and cooked until crispy on the outside and juicy within.
Habibi Kebs is a no-frills store specialising in authentic doner kebabs. The founders shared with us that they both have had prior culinary experience, and after a hiatus, they both decided to come together to start Habibi Kebs to bring the German doner experience to the masses. Contrary to traditional Turkish doner that’s served with rice, grilled vegetables, or tombik (AKA Turkish round pocket loaf) with little sauces and salads, German doner goes heavy on salad and sauces: all dressed and packed into bread for a portable, street-food-style sandwich.
The menu’s pretty straightforward: choose from three main styles, your protein of chicken, beef, or a mix of both, and a sauce: Garlic Sauce , Chili Sauce , or Herb Sauce . If you want it more saucy, you can top up $1 for an additional sauce.
If you’re feeling peckish, you can even upgrade your meal for an additional $5 , which comes with a side of fries and a soft drink.
We first got their signature Chicken Doner Kebab with Garlic and Chili Sauce ($11) . You get doner bread, AKA Turkish flatbread, stuffed with lettuce, tomatoes, jalapenos, red onions, red cabbage, and chicken, dressed in a spicy chilli and zingy garlic sauce.
The doner bread had a nice crusty exterior and a soft, fluffy interior, making the perfect base for the whole dish. The chicken was well marinated and slightly smoky, which complemented the fresh vegetables.
We also tried their Beef Durum with Garlic and Herb Sauce ($11) , which featured the same medley of lettuce, tomatoes, jalapenos, red onions, red cabbage, and grilled minced beef, drenched in a zingy garlic and herb sauce. The whole shebang was tightly wrapped in durum bread, similar to a burrito you’d get from Stuff’d.
The minced beef was nicely charred and finely minced, while the vegetables helped cut through some of its richness. I particularly liked how the durum was left under a press grill for a while, giving it a crunchy exterior for some textural contrast.
Worth noting: the owner mentioned that the minced beef is likely being phased out soon, so head down sooner rather than later if you want to try this combo.
Last but not least, we ordered the Mixed Doner Teller with Garlic and Herb Sauce ($14) . It featured a bed of golden-brown, thick-cut fries loaded with both aforementioned meats, lettuce, jalapenos, tomatoes, red cabbage, and red onions, then finished with a drizzle of garlic and herb sauces.
Usually, I’m wary of loaded fries as they tend to turn soggy fast. However, the fries here were still crispy on the outside and fluffy on the inside. They were generously loaded with toppings, and I particularly enjoyed how the vegetables and herb sauce helped to mellow out the richness.
We also had the opportunity to try one of their unreleased items: the Quesadilla ($12) , which featured doner chicken, mozzarella, and chili sauce encased in a tortilla wrap, and grilled till crunchy on the outside.
Without a doubt, this was our favourite dish of the bunch: cheesy and creamy, with a little kick from the chili sauce.
The release date is currently TBD, though the owner told us it could be as early as this month. So, do keep a lookout on their Instagram page for any updates.
Finally, we washed it all down with Salaam Cola ($3) , a soft drink hailing from Ireland that was refreshing on a hot day. It was sweet and fizzy, and tasted similar to Coke. The brand that produces Salaam Cola also donates 10% of their profits to conflict-afflicted regions.
Ambience at Habibi Kebs
The eatery is decked out in a vibrant red-and-white aesthetic reminiscent of an American diner. If you’re dining in, there are also a few chairs outside so you can sit down and enjoy your meal. You’ll definitely need it, as the interior of the store itself is squeezy with little ventilation, which isn’t an ideal condition for you to enjoy a sandwich in.
When we visited the store on a weekday lunch, there wasn’t much of a crowd, so we didn’t need to wait much for our food to arrive. However, the traffic did start to pick up after we got our food, so do come early if you’d like to skip the queue.
Habibi Kebs is located a five-minute walk from Kembangan MRT Station .
Habibi Kebs—Eatbook Review
…
summary: We tried Habibi Kebs, a muslim-owned eatery selling German-style kebabs from only $9, to see if it’s worth the trip.
title: This Muslim-Owned Eatery Sells German-Style Doner Kebabs From $9: Is It Any Good?

Dim sum buffets in Singapore
If you’re like me and would die happy with all the dim sum you could eat, Singapore offers plenty of dim sum buffets starting at just $ 1 6.80++ that are perfect for any occasion. Here’s a complete guide to affordable dim sum buffets in Singapore.
1. TungLok Teahouse
Image credit: @blurfoodie
TungLok Teahouse is a popular dim sum buffet option in Singapore among families, with its interior designed to create a convivial atmosphere to sip and chat over a good cup of tea. The A La Carte Dinner Buffet is priced at $26.80++ per person from Monday to Thursday, and $29.80++ from Friday to Sundays. There’s also the High Tea Buffet , priced at $16.80++ per person on weekdays and $21.80++ per person on weekends.
What’s better is that they are one of the few options for unlimited dim sum during dinnertime, which puts them head and shoulders above those catering to just the lunch and teatime crowd. Do note that a minimum of two people are needed to book a table for the buffet. Outside of dim sum, diners are entitled to Chinese delicacies such as their Chilli Prawn with Fried ‘Mantou’ on weekdays, Sweet and Sour Pork Chop on weekends and more.
Read our Tunglok Teahouse feature .
Address: 10 Sinaran Drive, #01-73, Square 2, Singapore 307506
Buffet hours: Daily 3pm to 5pm (High Tea Buffet), Daily 6pm to 10pm (A La Carte Dinner Buffet)
Tel: 6893 1123
Website
TungLok Teahouse is not halal-certified.

Image credit: Swatow Seafood
One might think seafood is the speciality of Swatow Seafood , but they are more commonly known for dishing out affordable dim sum. Drop by their Toa Payoh outlet for their High Tea Dim Sum Buffet that’s available daily at $ 33.80 ++ on weekdays and $38.80++ on weekends, with over 20 types of handcrafted dim sum selections, including crab and prawn dishes, and even a sweet treat to end your meal!

Located in Chinatown and Changi , Yum Cha Restaurant offers traditional Cantonese dim sum. Decked in marble tables and wooden chairs, Yum Cha brings back the nostalgia of a traditional dim sum teahouse. Order your favourite bite-sized dim sum buffet delicacies at their Changi outlet during their Weekday Dinner Buffet at $36.80++ per person . Popular picks include the Yum Cha Prawn Dumpling , Baked Mini Egg Tarts and Peking Duck Roll . If dim sum is not your thing, they offer other dishes such as Seafood Fried Rice , Stir Fry Ee Fu Noodle with Mushroom and more.

How the 1799 ScamShield Helpline functions
A quick look at the latest episodes of the Singapore Police Force’s educational Crimewatch series reveals a worrying trend: scams feature prominently in many cases. It’s a stark reminder of just how rampant such crimes have become, and how easily unsuspecting victims can fall prey to them.
But while scams in Singapore are becoming increasingly sophisticated, there are still ways to protect yourself. One of the most important tools at your disposal is the 1799 ScamShield Helpline . If something doesn’t feel right, simply dial 1799 for help. That call could make all the difference in protecting yourself and your loved ones from falling victim to a scam.
To see what goes on behind this crucial line of defence, we went behind the scenes for an exclusive look at the people and operations working round the clock to keep scammers at bay.
What is the 1799 ScamShield Helpline?
Launched in September 2024, the 1799 ScamShield Helpline is part of the ScamShield Suite, a joint initiative by the National Crime Prevention Council (NCPC), Singapore Police Force (SPF), and Open Government Products (OGP). It serves as a round-the-clock source of support for anyone who suspects they may be dealing with a scam.
Available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, it provides real-time guidance to help callers assess suspicious situations and decide on the best course of action .
Screenshot from: Mid-Year Scam and Cybercrime Brief 2026 by the Singapore Police Force
According to the SPF’s Mid-Year Scam and Cybercrime Brief 2026 , e-commerce scams were the most common type in the 1st half of the year, accounting for 23% of reported cases. Phishing scams came next at 18.5%, followed by investment and job scams at 13.4% each. Government official impersonation scams rounded out the top 5 at 8.1%.
With so many different ways scammers can catch people off guard, it’s little wonder that the 1799 ScamShield Helpline has handled over 310,000 calls since its launch , with another 500 or so coming in daily.
How does the helpline protect you from a scam?
With trained call agents on duty, someone is ready to help whenever you dial 1799. They are trained to help callers make sense of suspicious situations , spot potential red flags , and figure out the next appropriate steps .
The hotline also offers an automated option for scam victims to connect directly with participating banks . Callers who have fallen victim to a scam can select Option 1 from the automated menu and choose their respective bank to be transferred to a representative for further assistance.
Image credit: National Crime Prevention Council
While scams come in many different forms, most follow a similar playbook. Scammers often start by dangling an enticing offer, be it a too-good-to-be-true investment opportunity or even the promise of finding love.
Once they’ve earned the victim’s trust, they slowly crank up the pressure, using urgency, fear, or emotional manipulation to convince them to part with their money. And just like that, the money is gone, along with the scammer.
By calling 1799 before any money changes hands, you’ll have a better chance of spotting a scam before it’s too late. The guidance you receive can also help you recognise similar red flags in future, so you can look out for your loved ones and prevent them from falling into the same traps.
Inside the operations of the 1799 ScamShield Helpline
Image credit: National Crime Prevention Council
To keep pace with rising call volumes, the 1799 ScamShield Helpline moved its operations from Police Cantonment Complex to Certis’ facility in Bedok in July 2025. The move provided the helpline with more room to expand its operations and accommodate the growing volume of calls.
Today, Certis supports the helpline’s day-to-day operations to keep things running smoothly. More than 10 agents are stationed at the facility at any given time, with staffing levels adjusted according to call volumes.
Stepping into the office, I was pleasantly surprised by how cosy and calm it felt. Each agent had their own personalised cubicle, complete with noise blockers to help them focus amid what could otherwise be a hectic work environment.
Despite the multiple monitors and documents around the room, there was a surprising sense of calmness – quite a contrast to the potentially frantic calls coming through at any moment.
My experience as a ScamShield call agent
As part of the visit, I also got the rare opportunity to step into the shoes of a ScamShield helpline agent through a simulated call scenario. Despite receiving a quick briefing beforehand, I was still pretty nervous when it was time to answer the call.
On the other end of the line was a caller seeking help with a government official impersonation scam. He had been contacted by someone posing as a police officer, who claimed he was involved in a fake credit card scam and instructed him to transfer a sum of money.
…

Assurance Package 2026
Inflation has been hitting all of us hard this year, and it doesn’t look like things will get any better. Plus, we’re already in year 3 of the GST increase to 9%. To help tide us Singaporeans through these rough financial times, the Singapore Government announced a whole slew of measures meant to cushion these hits to our wallet. Enter the Assurance Package .
Here’s a quick primer on the Assurance Package if you’ve already forgotten: the Assurance Package is a series of cash payouts made to eligible Singaporean Citizens over 5 years from 2022-2026. Each payment is disbursed in December, and the 2026 edition can see you getting $100-$250 Keep on reading for all you need to know, whether you’re eligible or not, and what it means for you.
What is the Assurance Package?
The Assurance Package was first announced during Budget 2020, with a fund of $6 billion. Working in conjunction with the existing GST Voucher scheme, it’s intended to help defray the higher cost of living associated with a GST increase. There are 5 main components to the Assurance Package:
• Cash payouts . Singaporeans aged 21 years and over will receive cash payouts between $700 and $2,250, depending on their income and property ownership. These payouts will gradually be dispensed over 5 years from 2022 to 2026, in the month of December.
• CDC vouchers . Distributed to every eligible Singaporean household, these vouchers are redeemable at participating heartland shops and hawker centres, as well as major supermarkets and grocery stores , such as NTUC Fairprice, Giant, and Sheng Shiong.
• Senior’s Bonus cash payouts . Additional cash will be disbursed to seniors aged 55 years and above. The amount ranges from $200 to $300, and varies based on age group, income level, and property ownership.
• Additional GST Vouchers (U-Save) . Eligible households will receive additional U-Save rebates on top of those in the GST Voucher scheme. Meant to offset utility bills, the rebate amount credited depends on the size of your HDB flat.
• Medisave Top-ups . Singaporeans aged 20 years and below or 55 years and above will receive a Medisave top-up of $150 each year from 2023 to 2025, totalling up to $450.
Image credit: Unsplash
Assurance Package 2026 summary
These are the main Assurance Package benefits Singaporeans can expect to receive in 2026, as well as their corresponding eligibility criteria:

Who is eligible for the Assurance Package cash payout?
With more than 3 million Singaporeans qualifying for the Assurance Package cash payout, many of us must be wondering about the eligibility criteria, and how much we’ll be receiving exactly.
For starters, you have to be a Singaporean Citizen residing in Singapore, and aged 21 years and above in 2025 in order to be eligible for payouts in the first place.
The actual amount that you’ll receive is based on 2 factors: the number of properties you own and your Assessable Income (AI) for the year. The latter basically takes into account all the income you get from sources like your employment and rental income. To find out your AI, you can check your tax bill or Notice of Assessment on the IRAS website.
If you own more than one property, then you’ll just get either $100 or $200 annually over the 5 years, for a total of $700 for 5 years.
If you own just one property or none at all, then the next criterion to determine your payout amount is your AI.
If your AI is $39,000 and below, then you’ll receive the highest quantum from the Assurance Package, with payouts of $200-$600 over 5 years, amounting to a total of $2,250. If you have an AI of over $100,000, you’re considered a high-income earner and so will naturally receive lower payouts, of $100 or $200 for a total of $700.
Image credit: Ministry of Finance
Bear in mind that the AI for this upcoming Assurance Package payout is based on the Year of Assessment for 2025, and doesn’t scale with the years. This means that even if you got a significant pay raise in 2026 which brings you to a higher AI bracket, you’ll still be eligible for the bracket that you were in for 2025.
To find out more details about your own eligibility as well as the exact amount you’ll be receiving, you can login to the e-services online portal on the Assurance Package website with your Singpass account.
Image adapted from: GovBenefits
How can I receive the Assurance Package cash payouts?
Assurance Package Cash payouts will take place every December, until 2026. You can receive the cash in several ways.

Hooray! One last treat from the Government: eligible Singaporeans will receive up to S$250 in cash from 8 Dec 2026 . This enhanced Assurance Package (AP) will benefit around 3 million adult Singaporeans. It also marks the final cash disbursement under the enhanced Assurance Package, which was introduced to “help defray living expenses for Singaporean households, and provide more support for lower- to middle-income families”, the Ministry of Finance said in a statement released on 10 Nov 2026.
Between 2022 and 2026, those eligible for these payments will receive up to S$2,250 in AP Cash.
Credit -Corporate Finance Institute
So, who is eligible for the Dec 2026 AP Cash payout? Firstly, you have to be a Singaporean . Next, you have to be 21 years and older in 2027 . The Government determines your payout amount based on your Assessable Income (AI) and the number of properties you own. Your AI is based on your income earned in 2024, under the Year of Assessment 2025.
Singaporeans who own no more than 1 property will receive the following amounts:

You can check your eligibility here by logging into your SingPass. The Government will notify eligible recipients through the official gov.sg SMS Sender ID before and after crediting the AP Cash. Recipients do not need to apply for the payout. Those without a Singpass-registered mobile number will receive a letter at the address stated on their Singapore Identity Card.
You do not need to submit an application to receive the AP Cash. However, if you have not linked your NRIC to PayNow, link it by 24 Nov 2026 to receive your payout earlier. This is provided that your bank account is with one of the 16 participating banks in Singapore. Once done, you’ll be able to receive your AP Cash earlier, by 8 Dec 2026 .
If you haven’t linked your bank account to your NRIC or PayNow, but have a DBS/POSB, OCBC or UOB account, provide your account information at the govbenefits website by 30 Nov 2026 to receive the AP Cash via GIRO by 17 Dec 2026 .
Go get your AP Cash; more details are available on GOVBENEFITS and HERE .

summary: Singaporeans aged 21 and above in 2027 can receive between S$100 and S$250 in the final enhanced Assurance Package cash payout on 8 Dec 2026. The amount depends on assessable income for the Year of Assessment 2025 and property ownership, with different payment deadlines for PayNow-NRIC and GIRO recipients. The information is useful for eligible Singaporeans checking their payout amount and payment arrangements.
title: Up to $250 cash payouts for Singaporeans in Dec 2026

Champagniac , Singapore’s dedicated Champagne festival, returns this weekend on 14 and 15 November for its second edition. It has moved from Jewel Changi Airport to the Supreme Court Terrace at National Gallery Singapore .
Credit: Champagniac 2025
Popping champagne in a former courthouse sounds like an objection, but I’m sure even lawyers won’t mind as long as their glasses are full.
Credit: National Gallery Singapore
Last year’s debut drew 1,400 people. The pitch hasn’t changed: Champagne for everyone, not only the person at dinner who smells “ brioche ” without being asked. Led by Yeo Xi Yang — he’s the 2022 Singapore National Sommelier Champion and runs Convivial , Southeast Asia’s first dedicated Champagne bar.
Champagne houses and growers pouring at Champagniac 2026
Credit: Champagniac 2025
For a festival trying to make Champagne more accessible, they’ve managed to bring in some seriously good producers. Big houses like Billecart-Salmon , Pommery , Deutz and Jacquesson sit alongside the growers Champagne nerds go misty-eyed over: Egly-Ouriet , Larmandier-Bernier , Pascal Doquet . Then there’s Selosse Pajon , made by the grand-nephew of Jacques Selosse and pouring in Singapore for the first time. If that surname means nothing to you, the queue at that booth will explain it.
There’s sparkling from outside Champagne, too. Gusbourne and Roebuck Estates are flying the English flag, and Spain’s Bodegas Balmoral is there with its traditional-method Edoné range. It’s a good chance to test whether you can tell English fizz from French. I wouldn’t bet money on it.
What the S$98 ticket covers
A regular ticket gets you one three-hour session, an SKLO Linear N.1 glass to take home (valued at S$69) and one tasting per booth. Note the “one.” Some of the highlighted bottles are premium pours, paid for with tokens sold on-site at S$5 each. The festival hasn’t published the token prices for individual bottles, so it’s hard to know how much extra you’ll end up spending.
Is the Champagniac VIP ticket worth it?
VIP is S$198 and capped at 60 people per session. What you’re really paying for is access to the Glass Room , a private lounge with seating and eight premium cuvées personally selected by Yeo. These are rarer bottles from houses at the fair that won’t be poured on the main floor. Three he’s flagged are the Egly-Ouriet V.P. Grand Cru , Henri Giraud MV20 Aÿ Grand Cru and Jacquesson Cuvée 743 .
For an extra S$100, that’s eight pours you won’t find elsewhere at the festival, plus somewhere to sit down. If you were already planning to burn through tokens, VIP makes sense. If you just want to discover a few new champagnes and have a good afternoon, the regular ticket is enough. VIPs can also pay another S$60 for the Grower package or S$80 for the Grande Maison package.
Credit: Champagniac 2025
Masterclasses, art and everything else
There are three masterclasses, each capped at 24 seats and booked separately on top of a festival ticket. On Saturday at 2.30pm, Alexandre Collard runs a Collard-Picard session (S$68), and everyone goes home with a demi-bottle. Sunday’s 2.30pm slot is Champagne A. Bergère, also S$68. The Henri Giraud class (S$88) is on Friday’s preview night, which is for National Gallery members only.
There’s also a Champagne-and-watercolour workshop with French artist D’Gers, where you get to paint your own postcard. It’s free for the first 30 people each session and S$10 after that. German artist Míru is showing new work, and three DJs are on the decks.
Buy your tickets to Champagniac 2026
Address: Supreme Court Terrace, Level 4, National Gallery Singapore, 1 St Andrew’s Road, Singapore 178957
Dates: 14–15 November 2026 (members’ preview on 13 November, 7pm–10pm)
Sessions: 11am–2pm & 4pm–7pm, both days
Ticket prices: S$98 (Regular) or S$198 (VIP), plus S$5 tokens and S$68–S$88 for masterclasses
*Every ticket includes an SKLO Linear N.1 tasting glass (worth $69)

summary: Champagniac, Singapore’s Champagne festival, moves to National Gallery’s Supreme Court Terrace on 14–15 November. S$98 gets you a three-hour session, a SKLO glass and one pour per booth, with premium bottles on S$5 tokens. Look out for Selosse Pajon’s Singapore debut, Egly-Ouriet and Jacquesson. VIP (S$198, 60 per session) adds a private lounge with eight rare cuvées. Worth it if you were going to splurge on tokens anyway.
title: Champagniac 2026 – What $98 gets you at Singapore’s Champagne festival, now at National Gallery

Mister Donut has three Christmas donuts made with KitKat this year, sold at three for S$9.90 as a festive offer, or S$3.50 each at the usual price. The offer is for a limited time and while stocks last.
Two of the three are chewy donuts, and the third is a fluffy filled one.
The three KitKat donuts
• Holly Berry Wreath: a chewy ring dressed in strawberry chocolate, with a whole KitKat finger laid across the top.
• Frosty Choco Bauble: a fluffy donut filled with KitKat spread and wrapped in white chocolate, piped with red lines like a bauble.
• Merry Mint Garland: chewy donut halves filled with mint-infused KitKat spread and coated in mint chocolate.
Holly Berry Wreath, a chewy ring in strawberry chocolate with a KitKat finger. Image: Mister Donut Singapore
The Holly Berry Wreath contains wheat gluten, milk, soybean and egg, and no tree nut. The Frosty Choco Bauble and Merry Mint Garland both add tree nut, which matters for anyone buying a box for a children’s party.
Frosty Choco Bauble is filled with KitKat spread. Image: Mister Donut Singapore
Boxes and the donut tree stand
For orders, the chain’s online shop sells boxes of six at S$21. There is a box of each flavour and a Christmas Collection box with two of each.
There is also a Donut Tree Stand at S$8.80, a DIY tiered stand that holds 24 donuts.
The Donut Tree Stand costs S$8.80 and holds 24 donuts. Image: Mister Donut Singapore
Where to buy
Mister Donut, run in Singapore by RE&S, has 12 outlets: Anchorvale Village, Junction 8, Jurong Point, Northpoint City, Parkway Parade, Takashimaya Food Hall, Tampines 1, Thomson Plaza, Velocity@Novena Square, VivoCity, Waterway Point and 313@somerset. Most open from 11am to 9pm daily. Anchorvale Village is open from 11am to 9.30pm, Takashimaya Food Hall from 10am to 9.30pm, and VivoCity from 11am to 9.30pm on Monday to Thursday and from 10am to 10pm on Friday to Sunday.
Boxes and the tree stand are on order.misterdonut.com.sg for pickup or delivery.
summary: Mister Donut's Christmas range made with KitKat has three donuts at three for S$9.90 or S$3.50 each, boxes of six at S$21 online and an S$8.80 donut tree stand.
title: Mister Donut launches three KitKat Christmas donuts at three for S$9.90

body:
Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is a Chinese-style mutton soup stall at 115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre , with eager customers already forming a queue before it even opens for the day. Erm, well, not quite for the whole day. It operates for just 2.5 hours (11am – 1.30pm) , 5 days a week . With a rating of 4.6 stars out of 5 with a total of 369 reviews (at time of writing), it’s Singapore’s highest-rated mutton soup stall on Google Reviews .
A little voice in my head went, “It must be pretty darn good, eh?” This stall has also been awarded a Michelin Bib Gourmand for 9 consecutive years — that alone speaks volumes.
Naturally, my expectations were much higher than usual. As I stood in the queue, a rhythmic chopping sound echoed through the air, accompanied by a lady calling out and taking customers’ orders. As the fast-moving line gradually inched closer, the sounds that had been teasing my ears finally came into full view. From a conversation I couldn’t help but overhear, I gathered that the 2 ladies take turns swapping roles.
What to order at Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang
Most of the menu items come in 5 sizes, ranging from S$6 to S$10 , so there’s something suitable for every appetite. Just like the local saying goes, “Monkey see, monkey do.” I followed the lead of those queuing ahead of me and ordered the S$8 portion of the 羊杂 (mixed mutton) with a small bowl of Rice (S$0.40) .
For the price, I must say, the portion is pretty generous. There were pieces of mutton, 5 lamb balls, and lamb’s stomach bathed in a light brown soup, garnished with chopped Chinese celery.
The moment the soup hit my tongue, I was greeted by an unusual tingling sensation, accompanied by an almost siap siap mouthfeel. Its robust herbal profile brought to mind a hearty bowl of bak kut teh . It was definitely an acquired taste, and those who dislike herbal flavours may not appreciate it much. As someone who doesn’t mind herbal soups, I still felt that the flavour could be toned down a little to suit a wider audience.
The mutton here has got to be the Wagyu of its kind because, OMG, the meat was so tender that it barely required chewing, There was also no trace of unpleasant gaminess.
The lamb balls were firm yet smooth, and the overall texture reminded me of bouncy fishballs. It also packed a great flavour which wasn’t overly floury.
The stomach pieces were impeccably prepared, with a pleasantly clean flavour and none of that funky offal taste. I even found a couple of pieces of honeycomb tripe.
I then moved on to the S$8 bowl of 羊排骨汤 (mutton ribs soup) with rice as well. For S$8 , you’ll get about 7 to 8 substantial pieces of ribs. Much like the mutton from the previous dish, the rib meat was beautifully soft, with a pleasing balance of fat and lean meat.
For chilli lovers, I must say that this one is gentle enough for those who can’t handle too much heat, with a tangy profile reminiscent of the chilli commonly served alongside orh luak .
Who Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is best for
It’s perfect for herbal soup lovers who love something comforting for lunch. For those who avoid mutton like the plague because of its potential gaminess, Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang is a great place to start for its delicious, tender mutton; minus the strong taste.
How to get there?
115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre isn’t exactly near any MRT station. My recommendation would be to alight at Tiong Bahru MRT Station (EW17), get to the Opp Tiong Bahru Stn/Plaza bus stop, and board bus services that take you to Blk 116 .
Do we recommend Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang ?
If you love robust herbal flavours, then Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang will be up your alley. Mutton lovers who enjoy innards will appreciate the quality and softness of the lamb here. Oh, and I mustn’t forget the warm, friendly and efficient service here. It’s certainly the cherry on top!

summary: Chai Chuan Tou Yang Rou Tang at 115 Bukit Merah View Food Centre serves Chinese-style mutton soup with prices ranging from S$6 to S$10. Open for just 2.5 hours daily, 5 days a week, the Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognised stall is known for tender, non-gamey mutton, lamb ribs and innards in a robust herbal broth. It is particularly suited to herbal soup lovers and those looking to ease into eating mutton.

Tokyo’s iconic dessert sensation, Mr. CHEESECAKE , is officially debuting in Singapore with an exclusive pop-up at ION Orchard from 11 Nov to 30 Dec 2026 . Founded by acclaimed Chef Koji Tamura, the cheesecake brand has achieved legendary status — selling over 1 million whole cakes globally.
Prior to establishing Mr. CHEESECAKE, Chef Tamura built a distinguished career at world-renowned fine-dining establishments, including Mirazur and Restaurant ES in France. He also served as head chef at Tokyo’s TIRPSE, which is famous for receiving a Michelin star in the shortest time in the world.
Despite his impressive resume, Chef Tamura was most inspired by childhood memories of his mother’s home-baked treats and his own experience of baking a cake for a high school friend’s birthday. He began crafting cheesecakes late at night and sharing them on social media. The overwhelming online response eventually led him to depart from fine-dining kitchens and launch Mr. CHEESECAKE.
What sets Mr. CHEESECAKE apart from other cheesecake brands is its signature dual-layer construction that consists of a delicately baked top layer paired with a velvety, near-rare bottom layer. This unique construction is deliberate, allowing the flavours, aroma and mouthfeel of the cake to evolve with temperature changes and provide different sensory experiences with the same cake:
Frozen: Enjoyed straight from the freezer for a refreshing, ice-cream-like bite.
Half-Thawed (1–1.5 hours): Offers a dual texture with a frozen centre wrapped in a creamy outer coat.
Fully Thawed: Unlocks rich sweetness and aroma with a silky consistency akin to creme brulee.
We got to sample Mr. CHEESECAKE Matcha (S$69) , RICH TIRAMISU (S$69) and Mr. CHEESECAKE Sakekasu Coconut (S$69), served fully thawed. Do note that cakes are only sold whole and portions pictured in my article are tasting samples.
My favourite cake by far was Mr. CHEESECAKE Sakekasu Coconut , which carried sweet and floral tropical notes. This unusual combination pairs sake kasu with rich coconut and uplifts it with a touch of lychee puree. The sake kasu , which is the leftover pressed lees from sake production, brings a mildly yeasty and tangy flavour — akin to yoghurt — to the cake.
This gentle acidity pairs well with the smooth, buttery profile of the coconut and pleasant floral aroma of lychee, making for a complex and layered profile with depth without feeling too heavy or sweet.
Another offering that I thoroughly enjoyed was Mr. CHEESECAKE Matcha (S$69) . It might be too intensely earthy for casual drinkers like me, but dedicated matcha lovers are bound to adore it. It also features light, creamy mascarpone and a dash of vanilla to balance the richness and slight bitterness of the matcha. Despite the bold flavours of this cake, it remains remarkably light and enjoyable with just the right level of sweetness.
Finally, we moved on to the RICH TIRAMISU (S$69). Rather than a purely traditional tiramisu, Mr. CHEESECAKE’s version incorporates Japanese ingredients like hojicha , which imparted an earthy, roasted aroma.
Building on that roasted aroma, the addition of browned butter lends more depth and a slight nuttiness to the overall profile. In the middle sits a thin, crisp almond dacquoise layer to provide a textural variation from the mousse-like interior. However, for a tiramisu, I found it rather lacking in coffee flavours.
Driven by Chef Tamura’s humble ethos — “Not the world’s best, but we make your days the best” — this limited-time pop-up brings one of Japan’s most coveted pastries to local dessert enthusiasts. Make sure to head down between 11 Nov and 30 Dec 2026 to get a taste of his renowned cheesecakes.
13 best places to dine along Orchard Road & people watch [Oct 2026 update]
summary: Mr. CHEESECAKE’s limited-time pop-up at ION Orchard introduces Tokyo’s iconic temperature-evolving desserts to Singapore from 11 Nov to 30 Dec 2026. Featuring whole cakes priced at S$69 each, including signature variations like Sakekasu Coconut, Matcha, and Rich Tiramisu crafted by former fine-dining Chef Koji Tamura, the release targets local dessert enthusiasts seeking premium Japanese pastries. The tasting experience is ideal for readers looking to evaluate specific flavour profiles and texture transitions before purchasing whole cakes during the limited Orchard Road engagement.
title: 1 million sold — Tokyo’s Mr. CHEESECAKE pop-up opens in Singapore

Sin Siong Lim Sawmill in Sungei Kadut
While we might be colloquially known as the Little Red Dot, perhaps the moniker of “Garden City” is more apt when it comes to describing the sights in sunny Singapore. Take a look around, and you’ll find that the neatly manicured carpet of greenery extends even to the far reaches of the island, all thanks to proactive tree planting efforts in the 60s.
But as nature has intended, even the most colossal of trees cannot outlast the inevitable: the forward march of time, and in our land-sparse country’s case, urbanisation. So, in a metropolis so abundant with flora, where do the felled, leafy giants go? Enter Sin Siong Lim Sawmill , Singapore’s last operating sawmill.
The facility has been processing wood for well over a century, but they’re unfortunately being forced to shutter on New Year’s Eve. As part of OH! Open House ’s Departures programme, we were able to swing by the sawmill for a last look; here’s what we saw and learnt, from massive machinery to their impressive expertise in dealing with local lumber.
Where is Sin Siong Lim Sawmill & how can I visit it?
Sin Siong Lim Sawmill is located in the Sungei Kadut Industrial Estate in Kranji . It isn’t terribly difficult to get to, as it’s just a 4-minute walk from a nearby bus stop. However, since it’s an operational industrial facility, the sawmill is not open to the public for walk-in visits .
However, organisations occasionally hold tours that give the public a rare glimpse into facilities like Sin Siong Lim Sawmill. In OH! Open House ’s case, they not only provide educational tours through their Departures programme, but also partner with local artists who give their take on the history and significance of these spaces through creative installations.
Image credit: Roots
The latest edition of Departures featured visits to Sin Siong Lim Sawmill, while their pilot programme spotlighted Kelong E63, one of Singapore’s last working kelongs before it ceased operation in 2025. You can keep tabs on the OH! Open House’s website to sign up for upcoming tours, or give them a follow on Instagram or Facebook for more updates.
History of Sin Siong Lim Sawmill
It all began with Mr Lim Woon Khuan , a man with a zest for entrepreneurship who had arrived in Singapore from China in the early 1900s. After stints at a provision shop and shoe store, he then found work at Sin Siong Lim Sawmill, then known as Siong Lim Sawmill, and was eventually handed the reins.
What Syed Alwi Road looked like in 1972.
Image credit: National Archives of Singapore
The sawmill dates back to 1912, making it well over a century old. Interestingly, it wasn’t always relegated to the recesses of the North; it was originally located along Syed Alwi Road in Jalan Besar, an area which was also home to slaughterhouses, factories, and other industrial businesses.
The Song Lin Building at Syed Alwi Road, which stands at the site of the former Siong Lim Sawmill.
Image credit: Streetdirectory
The old sawmill premises withstood the storm that was WWII, and were used as an internment camp and screening centre to weed out anti-Japanese resistance during the war. In 1975, the sawmill then shifted operations to Sugei Kadut, where it still stands today.
Originally, the sawmill imported most of its wood, first from Sarawak, and then from Peninsular Malaysia. But the rising shipping costs and regional export restrictions of the 80s proved to be too strong a double whammy, and so Sin Siong Lim Sawmill had to look elsewhere closer to home for its supply of lumber.
How does Sin Siong Lim Sawmill operate today?
Our visit to Sin Siong Lim Sawmill began with a showing of local contemporary visual artist Robert Zhao Renhui ’s short film, Someone Will Come For You (2026). Screened within one of the sawmill’s lofty warehouses, the film juxtaposes the wails of mother nature against the buzz of chainsaws, as scenes of feeding birds and workers dissecting trees from branch to branch play out.
Accompanied by narration that was chanted rather than spoken, the film could prove a tad too avant-garde for the layman, but its underlying message remained resoundingly clear. If the recent plans to urbanise forested areas like Maju Forest , Gillman Barracks , and Tengah are anything to go by, the future of our local flora and fauna appears regrettably bleak.
Rampant deforestation’s one thing, but therein lies another quandary: what do we do with all the green waste in its wake? That’s where businesses like Sin Siong Lim Sawmill come in. Following their change in MO, the sawmill tapped into their decades’ worth of experience and became the de facto destination in Singapore for repurposing felled trees into usable timber.
Ms Lim showing the crowd a special ruler that they used back in the day to measure pieces of wood.
…
summary: Another dying trade is set to bite the dust.
title: Sin Siong Lim Sawmill: Singapore’s Last Operating Sawmill That Sprouts New Life For Felled Trees

Trevor Kam community MRT line walks
Most of us would consider the walk between an MRT station and the nearest bus stop enough cardio for the day. Trevor Kam , meanwhile, has been casually walking entire MRT lines across Singapore.
The 20-year-old “competitive MRT walker” has already conquered routes as long as 57km , sometimes spending up to 16 hours on his feet. His next and final target is the East-West Line (EWL) , which he plans to tackle on 13th November 2026 at 9pm .
Who is Trevor Kam & why is he walking every MRT line in SG?
Trevor Kam is a Singapore Permanent Resident with Australian citizenship who is currently waiting to enlist for National Service . He has dubbed himself a “competitive MRT walker”, and his goal is pretty straightforward: walk the length of every MRT line in Singapore within a day.
Image adapted from: sidequests central via Telegram, @trevuh2 via Instagram
It all ties into his love for side quests, AKA random adventures, that make everyday life a little less mundane. Trevor has said that he is often told there are no activities to do in Singapore , so he has made it his personal mission to make the country more exciting and enjoyable.
His side quests aren’t limited to putting his legs through hell either. He has previously learnt to breakdance, sung in front of an audience of 400 people, taken ice baths , and pranked people during Halloween by knocking on their doors.
View this post on Instagram
Before becoming a full-time content creator, Trevor worked for a media company in video content creation. He now documents his adventures online, on Instagram and TikTok . As of writing, he has 6,621 Instagram followers and 3,439 TikTok followers , with his sights set on reaching 10,000 followers by the end of 2026 .
He started with a 25.1km walk along the North East Line
Trevor’s MRT walking saga kicked off on 7th August 2026 , when he followed the North East Line (NEL) route. He covered 25.1km in 5 hours and 2 minutes , clocking more than 30,000 steps in the process.
Trevor with his day one supporter and friend, Bryan.
Image credit: sidequests central via Telegram
The NEL trek was the shortest of the routes he had planned at the time. While his friend Bryan Kow , a culinary student who helps Trevor map the walks, was supposed to join him, he wasn’t feeling well that day, leaving Trevor to solo the route.
Next came the Circle Line (CCL) later that month. This time, Bryan joined Trevor for the 47.19km journey, which took them 10 hours and 6 minutes and resulted in more than 67,000 steps.
Bukit Brown Cemetery.
It wasn’t exactly a seamless stroke. The pair somehow found themselves lost while walking from Caldecott to Botanic Gardens and ended up on the perimeter of Bukit Brown Cemetery . They had to quickly make a detour after spotting a warning sign against trespassing.
Trevor also had to contend with a 90-minute toilet break because of an upset stomach, plus an unexpected phone charging break at one-north so he could continue filming the journey.
50 people joined his 48km Downtown Line walk
Image credit: SAA Architects
Things got considerably bigger for his next challenge. On 21st August 2026 , Trevor set off to conquer the Downtown Line (DTL) , beginning his walk from Bukit Panjang MRT station at 7am.
The whole MRT-walking gang posed outside the Botanic Gardens.
Image credit: sidequests central via Telegram
The route covered roughly 48km and took him around 16 hours to complete. This time, the trek had evolved from a 2-man side quest into a community walk-a-thon. Prior to his walk, he made a post on his Instagram, encouraging folks to join him on his endeavour, with around 50 people joining Trevor on the big day.
Participants didn’t have to commit to the entire route either. They could join or leave the group at different stations, rest when needed, and even rejoin the walk later.
Participants even turned up in blue to match the DTL’s colour scheme.
Image credit: sidequests central via Telegram
Trevor has stressed that participants should go at their own pace rather than push themselves beyond their limits. After all, his own MRT adventures have previously left him with muscle aches, blisters and foot pain.
Over 80 people joined his longest walk yet along the TEL
Image credit: sidequests central via Telegram
Trevor levelled up again on 4th September 2026 , this time taking on the Thompson East Coast Line (TEL) . The trek stretched for around 57km and took approximately 16 hours , making it his longest MRT line walk yet, and more than 80 people in total joined in on the fun.
Image credit: sidequests central via Telegram
The growing community surrounding these walks has also spilled over onto Telegram. Trevor runs a channel called Sidequests Central , which has amassed a little over 1,800 followers as of writing.
The channel is where followers can keep tabs on his adventures and upcoming side quests, making what started as Trevor’s personal challenge a surprisingly large community affair.
…
summary: Can you walk the entire length of an MRT line in one day? Apparently Trevor Kam can.
title: This 20-Year-Old Is Walking Every MRT Line in SG, Join His Final East-West Line Trek On 13th November

Mala Mia is a new mala restaurant at Changi Airport T3
Image credit: love ling via Google Maps
Growing up, my parents told me two things certify someone as a “true Singaporean”: the ability to eat durians and handle spice. Though I haven’t really got around to the former, I can certainly still call myself a spice-loving Singaporean who’s obsessed with mala and all things spicy, and sometimes those cravings hit at the worst possible moment, like right before boarding a plane. If you suffer the same fate as I do, good news: Mala Mia is a new mala restaurant at Changi Airport Terminal 3 . It’s halal-certified, so Muslim spice fanatics can get their mala cravings fixed too.
Changi Airport Food Guide: 38 Places To Dine At Before Catching Your Flight
Image credit: Wenwen Kee via Google Maps
Start by picking your bowl of ingredients, priced at $2.90++ for 100g , with a minimum weight of 400g. Choose from over 60 ingredients, from familiar options like Beef Shabu and Prawns to unique additions such as Cheese Otah and Korean Fishcakes . You can even get some ingredients deep-fried A Hot Hideout-style, including their Lotus Root and Potatoes . Top it all off with their fluffy scrambled eggs for an additional $3++ .
Image credit: @dynolester
Choose your spice level, from Non-spicy for the spice-averse to Extra if you’re looking for a fiery kick. Then, pick your desired base. The classic Mala Stir Fry ($1++) is a safe option, while the Mala Collagen ($2.50++) features a spicy, slurpable soup that’s full of collagen. However, their standout is definitely the Mala Cream Base Dry ($1.50++) : a rich, glossy cream sauce packed with mala flavours, said to be reminiscent of Buldak Carbonara . If you’re not feeling the heat, you can opt for their non-spicy options, including the tangy Tomato Collagen ($2.50++) soup and Chicken Collagen ($2.50++) .
Image credit: Lim Yee Jing via Google Maps
Alternatively, you can try their Chongqing-inspired Mala Grilled Fish ($39.90++) in four different flavours: Mala , Tomato , Garlic Collagen , and Pickled Vege . Each dish features a whole fish simmered with enoki mushrooms, lotus root, tofu skin and more.
Image credit: @foodiedoodiewoodie
If that’s not enough, you can also order some of their sides to complement your mala bowl. Their La Zi Ji ($8.90++) AKA mala chicken is highly raved about, featuring juicy, batter-fried chicken pieces tossed with chillies and Sichuan peppercorns for an addictive snack. The Sichuan Pepper Corn Fries ($7.90++) are also a solid option: deep-fried corn ribs zhnged up with a punchy seasoning. There’s also free-flow mala popcorn for you to snack on in between meals.
Those on the hunt for new mala restaurants should check out Hi Bowl , a new malatang concept by beloved hotpot brand Haidilao. Otherwise, if you’re looking for more eats in the locale, our guide to 24-hour foods in Changi Airport has you covered for those red-eye flights.
Address: 65 Airport Boulevard, B2-49/50, Changi Airport Terminal 3, Singapore 819663
Opening hours: Mon-Fri 10:30am to 10:30pm, Sat-Sun 10:30am to 10pm

body:
Who doesn’t love a good loaf of bread? I know I can’t resist one, especially the crispy banh mi that originates from Vietnam. Recently, we got to try out Hi Bánh Mì at Geylang . I’ve realised that Geylang is filled with hidden foodie gems. The unassuming, old-school exterior of shop houses with rich architectural heritage really disguises the different types of food that you’ll find here.
Credit – Happy Belly Explorer via Google Reviews
Along the perimeters of 340 Geylang Road sits Hi Báhn Mì, which specialises in Vietnamese cuisine. Within its proximity are other Vietnamese-run stalls, from goldsmiths to salons. Like their stall name, the shop was simple and compact, simply greeting us with a gesture of “hi”!
To my pleasant surprise, Hi Bánh Mì also had low tables and chairs that added to the whole authentic Vietnamese experience. It was only during my recent trip to Ho Chi Minh that made me learn more about Vietnamese culture and how they’ve passed time.
Their national favourite pastime is people watching, which explains why you’ll see low stools scattered outside most cafes in Saigon. I loved how Hi Bánh Mì provided a glimpse of Vietnam all over again, especially with the pop music and native language filling up the background noise. What differentiates Hi Bánh Mì from other banh mi stalls in Singapore is the wide menu of 9 banh mi flavours.
What I tried at Hi Bánh Mì
Well, the only way to be certain that these banh mis are of quality is to try out signature flavours that taste similar to the ones I had in Vietnam. Hence, I opted for the Special Combination Banh Mi (S$8) and Roasted Pork Banh Mi (S$7) . Perhaps, these would be more familiar to our palates since they’re in the less experimental range.
During my meal, I noticed that the Special Combination Banh Mi was a common item that was constantly ordered. This is the best seller containing 4 kinds of homemade pork, freshly cured by Tammy, the owner. This process ensures control over flavours, allowing her to customise the salt levels of the meat.
Think of this option as a traditional banh mi in Vietnam, where you’d get all cuts of meat, from sliced ham to chopped cuts of cartilage. However, what sets them apart apart is the addition of pork floss that ties in nicely with the salty flavours of ham and crunchy bites of fresh radish and vegetables.
10 best Vietnamese food places in Singapore that will blow your mind
In addition, their homemade sauce and pate spread adds a sprinkle of sweetness into the whole meat-filled baguette — an elegant play of flavours.
Next, we have the Roasted Pork Banh Mi . I was really excited to try out this option because it contains pork belly, and who doesn’t love pork belly?
Just thinking about the layer of crispiness from the pork fat coming together with a bite of their crusty baguettes is making me salivate. Oh, this was great! To start, the buns had a perfect ratio of softness, crispiness and flakiness. They were fluffy in the centre and flaky on the outside, so when you take a bite, it isn’t difficult to chew.
This option was comparatively greener than the other, probably to balance out the flavours from their sinful choice of meat. I’m not complaining, though— the addition of coriander made the hearty pork belly more pronounced. The floral, earthiness of coriander acted as a foil to the rich meats, and the contrasting flavours made it even more addictive. I guess the saying of how opposites attract is reinstated in this scenario.
You’ll get slices of chillies inside if you opt for the spicy version. I particularly liked how this sandwich hit all aspects of spiciness, sweetness and saltiness.
And… We’re onto desserts! We had the Vietnamese Fried Bananas (S$3 per piece) , commonly referred to as goreng pisang . They’re almost the same thing, except Hi Bánh Mì adds sesame seeds into the coated batter.
Freshly made to order, these came in piping hot. The pure luxury of biting into the soft, melted banana brought me utmost joy. Every bite came with a golden crisp of fragrant twice-fried batter that blended nicely with the contrasting sweet flavours. As the self-proclaimed lover of anything banana-flavoured, I approve!
Final thoughts
Hi Bánh Mì is truly a hidden gem in Geylang. To let you in on my thoughts, I’m already thinking of the Beef Banh Mi or the spicy noodles ( bun bo hue ) in the secret menu that I would love to try out on my next visit. I was searching for them in the main menu, but apparently, these are secret menu items that only true regulars know about. Now, you’re in on the secret too.
Furthermore, at such affordable prices, you don’t even need to buy a ticket to Vietnam to appreciate their culture and food. Just grab a bun, sit on one of the stools, and watch the busy streets of Geylang at Hi Bánh Mì.
People also read:
Where can I find good steaks in Singapore?
Where are the best food in Geylang?
summary: Hi Bánh Mì at 340 Geylang Road serves 9 varieties of Vietnamese banh mi, alongside Vietnamese fried bananas and secret-menu dishes such as beef banh mi and bun bo hue. With banh mi priced from S$6 and a low-table seating setup, it is suited to diners seeking affordable Vietnamese food with a casual, local atmosphere.
title: Hi Bánh Mì: Hidden gem in Geylang with $6 banh mi & rustic vibes that remind you of Vietnam

body:
In my opinion, Korean fried chicken is the GOAT of fried chicken. While a lot of local spots do Korean fried chicken quite well, I’d love to try it at a place that originates from Korea. Luckily for all Eastsiders, famous Korean fried chicken chain Thunder Chicken is opening at Eastpoint Mall . The soft opening started on 6 Nov 2026 and their grand opening will be on 18 Dec 2026 . I won’t be surprised if they make it to your food delivery apps very soon as well.
Credit – Google
Thunder Chicken started in Seoul in 2006 . They built their brand on juicy, crunchy Korean fried chicken with a variety of flavours, and that rotation of flavours is a huge part of their success. After garnering more attention, they opened outlets in Busan. They have won 8 awards in Korea, which they display on their website.
From there, they have grown their brand to over 130 outlets worldwide, from Guam to Australia and now Singapore.
Credit – Thunder Chicken
You might be wondering why they call it Thunder Chicken. It’s actually because of the chicken crust. What makes Korean chicken so unique is the use of potato starch, which creates a thin and crisp layer. It is then double-fried to make it even crunchier. This is when the crust creates a lightning-pattern curl, giving the brand its name.
Credit – Thunder Chicken
Here’s what you can expect. They have regular Crispy Fried Chicken (S$13.90 for 3pcs) , which is normal fried chicken without any special sauces. Then there is the Flavoured Fried Chicken (S$15.90 for 3pcs) . This, to me, is the best option as it comes with a choice of 5 flavours (so far). You can choose between garlic , golden curry , green onion , Korean sweet and spicy and Sun of Hot . The names and flavours may change in the coming weeks, so do keep an eye on their website .
You can also expect classic Korean side dishes or banchan such as Tteokbokki (S$12.90) and Korean Steamed Egg (S$7.90) , and even Western favourites like Tater Tots (S$9.90) . Given its range of delicious chicken flavours and iconic side dishes, I won’t be surprised if Thunder Chicken is the next big thing in Singapore.
We tried Singapore’s highest-rated Korean fried chicken
summary: Thunder Chicken, a Korean fried chicken chain founded in Seoul in 2006, is opening at Eastpoint Mall (#01-12), with a soft opening from 6 Nov 2026 and a grand opening on 18 Dec 2026. Its Crispy Fried Chicken costs S$13.90 for 3 pieces, while flavoured options start at S$15.90, alongside sides such as tteokbokki. Suited to east-side diners looking for a Korean fried chicken option beside Simei MRT station.
title: Thunder Chicken – Award-winning Korean fried chicken storms Eastpoint Mall

Something Strange Festival Singapore 2026
Halloween may be over, but who says spooky season has to end in October? With Friday the 13th falling in November this year, there’s another excuse to indulge in all things creepy and mysterious.
Enter Something Strange Festival , Singapore’s first festival dedicated to horror, folklore, and the unexplained. It’s happening at Cineleisure from 13th to 15th November 2026 . Think haunted experiences, horror movie marathons, and conversations about the supernatural. And the Festival Village is free to enter, so you can get a taste of the strange without spending a cent.
How much are tickets to Something Strange Festival?
The good news is that admission to the Festival Village is free . But if you’re planning to catch a few horror movies or brave the haunted house, there are passes that come with extra perks.
Here’s a quick breakdown of your options:
• General Admission (Free): Access to the Festival Village, Main Stage talks, Curiosity Market, and selected Fringe activities.
• Festival Pass ($128): Includes 1 horror movie screening (U.P. $22), 1 Haunted House Experience entry (U.P. $20.70), discounted tickets for other activities, reserved Main Stage seating, priority queues, and 10% off F&B and shopping.
• All-Access Pass ($488): Includes Festival Pass perks, all 10 Horror-thon movies (U.P. $188), headline experiences, and exclusive backstage activities such as meet-and-greets and private sessions.
Free admission should be enough for those just dropping by out of curiosity. But for those planning to make a whole weekend of it, the Festival Pass or All-Access Pass could be worth considering.
Free things to do at Something Strange Festival
Hear about witchcraft, Thai horror & more at the Main Stage
Image credit: Something Strange Festival
If you’ve always been curious about the supernatural but would rather not come face-to-face with an actual hantu, head to the Main Stage at Basement 1. There’ll be free talks, performances, and demonstrations throughout the 3-day festival, covering everything from modern witchcraft to the history of horror films.
One of the more intriguing sessions is Roses Are Dark Spotlight , where practising Luciferian witch Phoebe of RosesAreDark shares her beliefs, discusses the ethics of charging for spells, and explains why some people choose to symbolically renounce their baptisms.
Meanwhile, at Thai Horror Through Film Posters , historian Shane Koh takes horror buffs through the evolution of Thai horror cinema from the 1970s to today. You’ll get to explore the country’s folklore and ghost stories through rare original film posters.
It’s not all ghosts and black magic, though. There’ll also be grunge, pop-punk, and acoustic music performances , plus a Soul Flow session on Sunday with Allisone and Jake for those looking to slow down and reconnect with themselves. It’s like a little spiritual cleansing after a weekend of spooky encounters.Admission for all of the above programmes is free , with reserved seating for Festival Pass and All-Access holders.
Browse The Curiosity Market & discover strange installations
Even if you’re not a fan of jump scares, don’t worry. You don’t have to consult a bomoh or dabble in the supernatural to enjoy the festival. There’s The Curiosity Market for shopping, where you can browse unusual finds and discover something a little out of the ordinary.
Image credit: Something Strange Festival
While you’re there, check out the festival’s Fringe programme , which brings interactive experiences and installations to different corners of Cineleisure. Some are free to explore as you wander around the Festival Village, while others require a ticket. So even if you’re not quite ready to step into a haunted house, there’s still plenty to poke your nose into.
Mingle with fellow supernatural enthusiasts at Social Night
Image credit: Something Strange Festival
After a full day of ghost stories and paranormal encounters, you might want to unwind with a drink or two. On 14th November, the festival is hosting Social Night at Ceni Bar & Kitchen on Level 1, where you can mingle with fellow horror buffs, festival creators, and guests over drinks, music, and live performances.
Swap ghost stories or just enjoy a night out with like-minded folks – here’s a chance to keep the festivities going after dark. Entry is free, although you’ll have to pay for your own food and drinks. You can also reserve a table if you’d rather secure a spot beforehand.
Paid experiences at Something Strange Festival
Get spooked at the Haunted Backrooms, with or without jump scares
If Halloween Horror Nights didn’t give you enough scares this year, Haunted Backrooms by Movie Mania might just do the trick. Think dimly lit corridors, creepy rooms, and scare actors lurking around corners, ready to make you regret stepping inside.
Image for illustrative purposes only.

title: Something Strange Festival: Celebrate Friday The 13th With Free Talks On Supernatural & A Curiosity Market

body:
Ampang may be best known for its quiet neighbourhoods and embassy-lined roads, but tucked between the hills and high-rises lies a treasure trove of flavour. From the smoky grills of Thai street eats to bubbling pots of Korean stew, from golden plates of nasi kuning to sizzling Chinese stir-fries and spice-laced Middle Eastern feasts— this corner of Klang Valley is a culinary crossroads in every sense.
We went fork-first into the heart of this city to bring you a list of tried-and-true favourites. Here’s my 9 solid eats in Ampang that serve up the kind of meals that linger long after the last bite.
Name
Location / Area
Key highlight
Fox Paradox Cafe
The Grange, Jalan Ampang
Blueberry Cheese Sourdough Toastie
B.station

Chicken Tangsuyuk and Korean stews

1. Fox Paradox Cafe
The Grange @Ampwalk has become my latest fixation, and right behind its doors is Fox Paradox Cafe . I’m writing this fresh from my second visit in as many days to this JAKIM-certified halal spot . Consider this your cue to check it out.
Now, pricing leans toward the premium side. For the best introduction to Fox Paradox, start with their breakfast and brunch offerings, especially the toasties. My top pick is the Blueberry Cheese Sourdough Toastie (RM30) .
Imagine thin slices of sourdough, toasted to a crisp golden crust, sandwiching a generous smear of blueberry jam that practically oozes with every bite. Sweet mango slices add to the tart-sweetness, while cream cheese and cheddar bring in a creamy, savoury richness. A light dusting of powdered sugar finishes it off like a delicate snow.
As for mains, they’re more of a work in progress to me. But if you’re hungry, the Beef Brisket Aglio (RM42) is your best bet: linguine tossed with a tomato-based brisket ragu , caramelised onions, crispy cauliflower, and a silky egg yolk.
Drinks-wise, 2 must-tries: the Iced Earl Grey Cinnamon Coffee (RM17) and the Date Coconut Frappuccino (RM16) . While the execution could be a touch more polished, the flavours are delightfully addictive.
G02-G03, The Grange, 218, Jln Ampang, Kampung Datuk Keramat, 55000 Kuala Lumpur
Daily: 8am – 8pm
Instagram | Website
2. B.station
Credit
Established in 2009, B.station in Jalan Ampang Utama has been my go-to for Muslim-friendly Korean comfort food. Tucked away in a modest little space, it feels less like a restaurant and more like walking into a friend’s home.
The menu offers a variety of selections, from à la carte staples to hearty set meals. But the dish I always return to is the Chicken Tangsuyuk (RM38) . It’s the real deal: starchy-crisp batter that’s slightly chewy on the outside, tender chicken within, all drenched in a glossy sweet and sour sauce that hits the spot every time.
If you’re coming with a few friends, I’d recommend adding the Sundubu Jjigae (RM32) and Tteokbokki (RM18) to the table. Both are rich, gochujang -based dishes that are best enjoyed with a bowl of hot, fluffy short-grain rice.
C14-1, Jalan Ampang Utama 1/1, Taman Ampang Utama, Ampang, 68000 Kuala Lumpur
+6016 201 0124
Daily: 11.30am – 10pm
Facebook | Instagram
3. Sweetree Restaurant
Credit – Sweetree Restaurant
If you’re wondering why I’m sharing two Korean spots back to back— well, it’s simple. Some folks are perfectly fine with Muslim-friendly eateries, while others prefer a place with full JAKIM Halal certification. So here you go: another worthy addition to the list but this time, fully certified.
Sweetree Restaurant has long been a dependable favourite, and when it comes to comfort food, my usual picks are the Sundubu Jjigae (from RM27.90) , the Chikin Tangsuyuk (RM31.90) which is available in both the classic crispy batter or the traditional chewy rice version, and the Samgyetang (RM79.90) for those days when you need something nourishing and a little splurge-worthy.
If Korean BBQ is more your style, Sweetree delivers the real deal. You can go for a full BBQ Set or mix and match two BBQ Plates, then add on any extras you like from the à la carte menu.
…
summary: Ampang’s dining scene spans Korean comfort food, Kedah-style nasi kuning, Chinese-Muslim seafood, Thai BBQ and Middle Eastern cuisine, with established eateries covered across the neighbourhood. Options range from casual meals around RM19 to premium steaks and seafood, with both halal-certified and Muslim-friendly venues alongside non-halal choices, making this a useful reference for diners exploring Ampang’s varied food scene.
title: 9 best eats in Ampang to take your taste buds on a global tour

A month ago , we found out that Age.3 was coming to Singapore sometime in November . The Japanese fried sandwich (sando) store , which has drawn queues of up to 2 hours at its Ginza outlet, first opened in 2023.
Since then, they’ve expanded to locations around the world and sold more than 1 million fried sandwiches. And now, their viral fried sandos have finally landed in our island city at ION Orchard .
We got to try some of Age.3’s popular items ahead of its opening on 13 November 2026 , and let’s just say – we’re officially fans. The hype was definitely justified, especially as a bread lover myself! Keep reading to find out what we tasted and loved!
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
Age.3 is known for its golden-fried milk bread that is fried and filled to order. That hasn’t changed for its Singaporean outlet at B4 of ION Orchard . The result is fresh bread in your hands that is crisp on the outside but soft and chewy on the inside.
To me, the milk bread itself was consistently one of the best parts of Age.3’s sandos. The initial crunch and the softer texture that follows, combined with its delicately sweet, milky flavour and savoury richness from frying, make every bite really satisfying.
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
The fried milk bread, however, is only half the magic. The other half comes in the form of Savoury and Sweet fillings , of which there are 35 to choose from. We went for the brand’s most popular Crème Brûlée (S$7.80) and 2 other beloved flavours: Grilled Cheese with Smoked Salmon (S$9.80) and Ganache (S$7.80) .
Crème Brûlée was definitely our favourite, with its custard whipped cream filling and flame-torched, caramelised sugar layer on top. The sweetness of the brittle, crunchy topping and smooth, rich filling complements so well with the toasty notes of the milk bread.
This is a flawed comparison, but it reminded me of butter-sugar toast – on steroids. There’s no question why this item is number 1 on the menu.
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
The other sweet option we tried was Ganache . It tastes exactly how it looks – a chocolate lover’s dream. Inside, you’ll find a rich, indulgent chocolate cream . At the top, you’ll find another layer of chocolate powder and rich nama chocolate cubes .
This interesting flavour felt most like a dessert out of the 3 options we ordered. If you have a sweet tooth, this is for you.
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
If the Ganache Sando is the closest to a dessert, the Grilled Cheese with Smoked Salmon Sando is the closest to a small meal. We had zero regrets ordering this one. On top, there is smoked salmon , melted cheese , and avocado . But underneath, there is a hidden surprise – potato salad filling !
Every bite gives you a burst of flavour with a savoury punch, without being overwhelming. If you want something more substantial to fill your stomach, we highly recommend this one.
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
If you’re already convinced and want to try these fried sandos yourself, head down early. Beyond the potentially long queue, Age.3 will also be holding an opening promotion from 13 to 15 November 2026 . The first 100 customers each day will get to purchase a Whipped Cream Sando for just S$1 instead of the usual S$4.80.
I’m definitely planning another trip down to Age.3 with friends soon, and trying other flavours next time I’m at ION Orchard . For a closer look at the delicious fried sandos, watch the video below:

Jisoo : Click In Singapore pop-up store
BLINKs, get ready to make some room in your merch collection. BLACKPINK’s JISOO is bringing her CLICK pop-up to The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands from 13th to 29th November 2026 , complete with exclusive apparel, adorable bear-themed collectibles, and plenty of photo opportunities.
Organised by CK Star Entertainment and JISOO , the pop-up will be circus-themed, based on her recent music releases, CLICK and ADDICTED . There’s also a sweet treat in store for fans, as Singapore will be the 1st country worldwide to get their hands on JISOO’s new POPPOP popcorn , with prices starting from just $6 .
If the Hello Kitty x BLACKPINK Jisoo pop-up earlier this year is anything to go by, you’ll want to be there on day 1 to get your hands on your favourite merch.
What can I expect at the pop-up?
Step into Jisoo’s circus-themed pop-up
Image credit: @ckstar.sg via Instagram
Fans who have been keeping up with JISOO’s recent releases will recognise the playful circus aesthetic at the CLICK pop-up. Held at the Digital Light Canvas on Level B2 of The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands , the space brings elements from CLICK and ADDICTED to life.
Image adapted from: @sooyaaa__ via Instagram
Expect a colourful setting filled with circus-inspired details, making it a spot to snap a few photos before browsing the merchandise. The pop-up has previously made appearances in Seoul and California, and now Singaporean BLINKs can join in on the fun.
Image adapted from: @sooyaaa__ via Instagram
Do note that entry is strictly by reservation , so you won’t be able to simply walk in. Reservations can be made via Klook from 10am on 12th November 2026 , ahead of the pop-up’s opening.
Shop Singapore-exclusive merch & bear-themed collectibles
If you’ve been looking to expand your BLACKPINK merch collection, there’ll be plenty to browse here. The pop-up features a range of apparel, accessories, plushies, and stationery, including a couple of items made exclusively for Singapore.
Image credit: @ckstar.sg via Instagram
For starters, fans can pick up the Singapore Exclusive T-Shirt ($66) or Singapore Exclusive Zip-up Hoodie ($120) . Both come in free size, so you can rep your favourite BLACKPINK member with merch that’s only available at the Singapore pop-up.
Image credit: @ckstar.sg via Instagram
There are also T-shirts ($66) featuring artwork and bear designs, alongside CLICK x SHUMON Pajamas ($99) for fans who prefer something cosier.
Image credit: @ckstar.sg via Instagram
Those looking for accessories can check out the Caps ($50) , available in bear and CLICK logo versions.
Image credit: @ckstar.sg via Instagram
As for collectibles, the JISOO Plush Doll ($83) and CLICK Baby Bear NFC Version ($53) are among the standout items. There are also smaller keepsakes such as the Bear Plush Pouch ($31) and Blind Box Keyring ($14) , with the latter being one of the more wallet-friendly souvenirs.
Image credit: @ckstar.sg via Instagram
Photocard collectors can grab a Photocard Binder ($24) or CLICK x SHUMON Photocard Holder ($24) to store their favourite pulls. Other merchandise available includes bags, stationery, home accessories, and more.
Be among the 1st in the world to try Jisoo’s POPPOP popcorn
Here’s something Singaporean fans can brag about: JISOO’s POPPOP popcorn will be making its worldwide debut right here in Singapore. Each packet costs $6 , with 15 flavours to choose from.
Image credit: @ckstar.sg via Instagram
The range goes beyond your usual sweet and salted popcorn. Fans who enjoy savoury snacks can try flavours such as Sweet Corn , Pizza , Tteokbokki , Seaweed , Wasabi Mayo , and Cheese Onion .
For something with a little more kick, there are Mala , Buffalo Wing , Perilla Oil Stir-Fried Kimchi , and Salted Egg flavours. You’ll also find Butter Shrimp and Tomato among the options.
Those with a sweet tooth can look forward to Honey Hotteok , Apple Pie , and Brown Sugar Milk Tea flavours. With such an unusual lineup, you might find yourself leaving with more popcorn than you originally planned.
Visit the Jisoo Click pop-up store at Marina Bay Sands
With exclusive Singapore merchandise, plenty of bear-themed collectibles, and the global debut of POPPOP popcorn, the JISOO CLICK pop-up is shaping up to be a treat for local BLINKs.
The pop-up runs until 29th November 2026 , so there’s a little over 2 weeks to check it out. Just remember to secure your reservation on Klook before heading down, as entry is available by booking only.

Science Centre Singapore
If your last visit to Science Centre Singapore was on a school excursion, you’re long overdue for a return trip. Besides the classic exhibits you’ll remember from your childhood, there are seasonal exhibitions that change throughout the year, giving you something new to look forward to each time.
It’s a solid pick for couples seeking an unconventional date, families with curious kids who may be budding scientists, and solo explorers alike. Here’s our complete guide to Science Centre Singapore so you can jam-pack your visit with all the highlights.
Things to do at Science Centre Singapore
Permanent exhibitions
Science Centre Singapore houses a series of permanent exhibitions that are no less delightful on subsequent visits. It’s actually very nostalgic and comforting to return to the same exhibitions over different chapters of your life, and see how you can take in familiar showcases with fresh eyes and a new perspective.
Enter Science Centre Singapore’s lobby and be greeted by The Mind’s Eye , a collection of optical illusions and trick-shot photo ops. Expect to be equal parts confused and trigger-happy, with plenty of snaps that your friends will be asking about in the comments.
Image credit: Science Centre Singapore
As you can well infer from the name, Everyday Science reveals the science behind things you see daily, like why the sky is blue and how rainbows form. You’ll also get to try out levitating balls and invisibility shields, and navigate foggy streets with a flashlight in a night-time zone.
Everyone’s favourite WhatsApp sticker character Quby has made a home at the Everyday Science gallery, popping up across the space to make everyday science concepts feel a little more approachable. Discover science together with cheerful explorer Quby through fun, hands-on experiences and exclusive merch.
The award-winning Phobia: The Science of Fear exhibition digs into the psychology and physiology of fear, and why it affects us the way it does. Brace yourself for the coffin-themed Buried Alive exhibit, or test your nerves in a simulated public speaking session in front of an audience. We won’t spoil the experience for you, but jumpscares are lurking at several corners.
Know Your Poo is exactly what it sounds like, a cheeky exhibition all about human waste, toilets, and the surprisingly intriguing history and science behind sanitation. Compare your business against the Bristol Stool Chart, learn why farts smell in the Cheeky Fart Chamber, and pose on a porcelain Royal Throne for a photo that’ll definitely get people talking.
Image credit: Science Centre Singapore
Savage Garden takes you through a whimsical village of carnivorous plants, complete with a theatre show where larger-than-life plant characters sing and gossip about their favourite foods. Afterwards, spot real carnivorous plants in a live tank, or take a ride down a giant pitcher plant slide. Who knew learning about plants could involve sassy animatronics and playground fun?
Image credit: Science Centre Singapore
Here’s one that’s visually awe-inspiring, and will inspire a fascination with cinematic history as well. A zoetrope is an early pre-film animation device that creates the illusion of motion using a sequence of static images or 3D figures.
Science Centre Singapore’s Giant Zoetrope enhances this animation method with strobe lights, “tricking” your brain to interpret the individual 3D static images as a single moving image.
Image credit: Science Centre Singapore
Singapore’s reputation as a Green City is known far and wide, and Urban Mutations is where you can find out how cities all over the world adapt and function. Discover hidden systems, clever solutions, and even tensions that come with rapid growth. You might just walk away with a newfound appreciation for something as simple as your daily commute.
Image credit: Science Centre Singapore
Some Call It Science is all about learning by doing, with hands-on stations where you can play with magnets, light, and sound like a real scientist. You can also challenge a friend to Science Kombat, an arcade-style game where you battle using “superpowers” inspired by famous innovators.
Image credit: Science Centre Singapore
The Tinkering Studio lets visitors young and old get hands-on with simple builds, from designing light flying creations to send gliding over a wind table, to piecing together a path for a marble to roll from top to bottom. There’s also a pinball machine where you set up your own obstacles and see how many bells you can ring before the ball stops.
Image credit: Science Centre Singapore
Prepare to be guilt-tripped – albeit for a good cause – over at Climate Changed . There’s an interactive show where you become a “Climate Change Agent”, and a quiz-style game called Guilt Trip that tests how eco-friendly your lifestyle really is.
Image credit: Science Centre Singapore
