With the most entertaining Christmas games, you won’t have to worry about your party being a snooze fest. Now that you’ve got dinner ready, loaded up on Christmas desserts and decorated the tree, it’s time to start planning the entertainment. Let’s put the jolly in festive parties by hosting fun and unique Christmas-themed games that’ll have everyone in stitches, going ho ho ho… Oh, and if you’re hosting Secret Santa this year, here are some Christmas gift ideas in Singapore .
Cool Christmas games for any party
1. Escape the North Pole!
Can you escape?
Oh no, you’ve been trapped in the North Pole! What are you going to do? If you’ve got a group of board game-loving friends coming to visit, add this to your collection. This tabletop escape room will have you deciphering clues and solving puzzles to save Christmas. Put your Santa hats on because you’re gonna be doing some serious thinking.
How many players: Good for up to six players for two to three hours of fun
What do you need: You can grab the Escape the North Pole board game online!
2. Guess that Christmas song
Are you the kind of person who loves listening to every trendy song? Put your knowledge to the test with blind karaoke. All you need is a speaker and a phone or a smart TV so everyone can join in the fun. Look up any Christmas song or shuffle a bunch of them on a playlist, and get everyone to guess the tune before the lyrics start!
How many players: At least two. If you have a big group, split up into teams!
What do you need: A good speaker so everyone can hear – get a big screen to turn it into karaoke!
3. Never Have I Ever, but make it Christmas
Photography: Julia Larson via Pexels
Here’s a familiar game: each person takes turns to say something they’ve never done, and those who have must carry out the penalty. Give this a Yuletide twist by adding ‘Christmas’ to every ‘Never Have I Ever’ statement, and consider getting party-goers to take a sip of hot chocolate or a bite of their log cake to make it festive (and family-friendly).
How many players: Best done in a group of at least four
What do you need: Just yourselves and an app to help generate questions in case you get stuck.
4. Christmas Movies as Emojis
Do you and your party guests love Christmas movies ? Welcome to the club. Go ahead, make a list (and check it twice) of classic and cool new festive flicks. Turn ’em into cute emojis and see who’s the first to guess them correctly.
How many players: Teams of three or more!
What do you need: A game master willing to translate movie titles into emojis, and a screen to present the prompts
5. Who’s the Best Bartender?
Photography: Tim Douglas via Pexels
If you’ve got bar tools and liquor bottles at home, get your dinner guests in on the action. Have everyone take turns to shake up their best Christmas-themed cocktail, then vote for their favourites. All your boozy drinks for the night will be sorted, and they’ll be kept entertained – it’s a win-win!
How many players: As many as possible for all kinds of unique drinks!
What do you need: Your favourite liquors of choice, fruit, and mixers. Bar tools are fantastic to add to the vibe, but not necessary
6. Christmas Trivia Night
Photography: Kevin Malik via Pexels
Nothing gets the competitive spirit going like a good trivia night ! All it takes is one Google search to find lists of fun Christmas-themed questions. Split yourselves into pairs or even groups, and your host can help facilitate. If you want to make it extra fun, create a festive slideshow with all the questions. Or put everything into Kahoot for that added time-based stress.
How many players: At least four – split yourself up into teams or take on the quiz individually
What do you need: Someone to prepare questions and facilitate the quiz, or to create the Kahoot game
7. The Christmas Murder Game
Gasp, Rudolph’s been murdered! That means the rest of the elves have to sit in a circle and keep their eyes closed (it’s the night of Christmas Eve, after all). You know how it goes: the murderer awakens to secretly “kill” someone by winking at them. After the killer has chosen the victim, it becomes Christmas morning. Now, everyone opens their eyes and tries to pinpoint the culprit. But each time someone accuses the wrong elf, the killer gets to choose another victim the next night. Get your detective cap on for a thrilling party night!
How many players: We find this game best played in large groups, so you can have two murderers. Eight players and up is a great amount.
What do you need: A game master to pick the murderers and instruct everyone. You can also use free Telegram bots to help facilitate the game and even get new unique roles!
8. Jingle Bells Toss
Photography: Rodnae via Pexels
Beer pong, but make it Christmas. All you need are reusable cups and loads of jingle bells. Split into two teams and try your best to toss all the bells in the cup within a minute. The team that loses… well, make ‘em do an embarrassing forfeit!
…

New cafes in Singapore with good food for 2026
New aesthetic cafes open in Singapore almost every week, but not all are worth a trip beyond the Instagram photo. This year, we’ve been looking for the ones that put the food first, whether it’s a proper brunch, a standout pastry, or a dessert you’ll want to order again. Here are 10 new cafes in Singapore that opened in 2026 , all serving good food that’s actually worth coming back for.
21 Beautiful Cafes In Singapore For Korean Cube Croissants, Matcha Desserts And More
1. Shared Table
Tucked inside Ang Mo Kio-Bishan Park is Shared Table , a gorgeous garden cafe with nourishing brunch plates. The cafe opened in mid-September 2026 to much fanfare, as it’s also run by the owner of Average Service in Jalan Besar.
The star dish is the Nourish Plate (from $21.90++) , which gets you one grain bowl, one protein, two sides, and a soup of the day. Healthy food sometimes has a reputation for being bland, but that isn’t true here—the Honey Glazed Goji Smoked Duck comes highly recommended with its sweet-savoury glaze, and the Honey Miso Salmon features a house-made honey and miso blend.
Their sides aren’t an afterthought either—our favourites are the Hummus with Roasted Mushroom ($18.90++) and Chicken Skewers ($14.90++) , served with tzatziki and warm pita.
Read our Shared Table review .
Address: Ang Mo Kio-Bishan Park, 1382 Ang Mo Kio Ave 1, Singapore 569932
Opening hours: Daily 11am to 10pm
Website
Shared Table is not halal-certified.
Average Service Founder Opens Garden Cafe In Bishan-AMK Park—Here’s Our Review
2. Noci Bakehouse
After the queues at their Suntec City flagship, Noci Bakehouse built on that buzz with a second outlet at Orchard Gateway . In place of shio pan, the Orchard outlet focuses on Korean bagels, available in 13 sweet and savoury flavours, alongside a small selection of house-made cream cheeses.
Image credit: @nocibakehouse
An outlet-exclusive is the wood-fired panuozzo, an Italian sandwich bread made to order. On our visit, we had the Bulgogi Panuozzo ($18) and Burrata Jambon Panuozzo ($23) , which stacks ham with a whole ball of burrata on top.
Read our Noci Bakehouse feature .
Address: 277 Orchard Road, #01-09/09A, Orchard Gateway, Singapore 238858
Opening hours: Daily 8:30am to 8:30pm
Website
Noci Bakehouse is not halal-certified.
Popular Korean Bakery Opens In Somerset With Wood-Fired Italian Sandwiches
3. Elijah Pies
Image credit: Elijah Pies
Elijah Pies ’ third and largest outlet is a 60-seat flagship that opened in September 2026, taking over a 96-year-old heritage shophouse in Joo Chiat . Fans of the cafe have to order their newly launched Pizza Pies , which are six-inch pies meant for sharing. These decadent pastries are made using laminated dough with 27 layers of French butter, and are baked over a three-day process.
Image credit: Elijah Pies
Flavours include Garlic Ebi ($22++) , Truffle Croque ($24++) , Cheeseburger ($23++) , and Ruffles ($23++) , which is inspired by sour cream and onion chips. For dessert, the Kaya Toffee Pie ($9++) has housemade pandan coconut jam over a hidden layer of gula melaka toffee, while the Souffle Pie ($18++) features chocolate souffle with a warm gianduja centre.
Read our Elijah Pies Joo Chiat feature .
Address: 72 Joo Chiat Place, Singapore 427789
Opening hours: Daily 10am to 10pm
Website
Elijah Pies is not halal-certified.
Elijah Pies Opens Third Cafe In A Joo Chiat Shophouse With Outlet-Exclusive Kaya Pie

If you’re a die-hard ice cream and waffle fan, you’ve probably heard of FreakyCones , a popular cafe in Chinatown with an impressive 4.9-star Google rating from over 1K reviews. In July 2026, they launched FreakyNoods Pasta , a new pasta concept on the second floor of their shophouse cafe!
Image credit: FreakyNoods
You can look forward to a small selection of affordable pasta mains here, all priced under $20+ and served in generous portions. Our favourites include Prawn Hub ($16.90+) , an aglio olio dish topped with torched whole prawns, and Beef Daddy ($15.90+) , a Japanese-inspired bolognese featuring a rich, umami-packed beef sauce elevated with garlic confit butter. Don’t miss out on the coffee, either; they serve a mean White ($6+) that’s silky and robust.

body:
Most Nyonya eateries in the city settle for pretty facsimiles of heritage. A few framed portraits here, a vase of batik flowers there, and suddenly you’re meant to feel like you’re no longer in KL circa 2026.
Limapulo Terrace , however, is no mere imitation. Tucked inside Tong Shin Terrace in Bukit Bintang , a preserved 1930s building, it feels like stepping through a doorway into a story that’s still unfolding.
Tong Shin Terrace itself deserves a pause. Once a grand residence, now it serves as a cultural custodian, home to both Limapulo Terrace and Omah Jawa . Together, they narrate the conversation between Peranakan and Javanese traditions.
On the ground floor, wooden beams and soft shadows create a dining room that feels both classic and intimate. Venture deeper and you find an alley that could be mistaken for a Mediterranean daydream, the kind of corner where time seems happy to linger. Reminiscent of children’s laughter and languid motions of life during warm summer nights.
A left turn takes you to a mysterious staircase with stories tucked into its worn steps; another path reveals kebayas for rental, complete with accessories and fragrances that tempt you to carry a piece of this world home.
Upstairs is where nostalgia gathers. The architecture still hints at its cinematic past, with forgotten corridors and rooms holding antique chairs that seem to whisper of their former owners.
A spiral staircase coils elegantly into the centre, leading to a landing where a cat might nap undisturbed by history or visitors. Around it, a smoking nook and original tiles from 1937 stand like quiet witnesses of timeless regality.
Anyway, I hope you enjoy the little house tour from your personal guide (regrettably not Sabrina Carpenter …). Let’s get to feasting!
What I tried at Limapulo Terrace
I started with Limapulo Terrace itself, naturally drawn to their Michelin Guide star, the Nyonya Laksa (from RM18) . The steaming bowl arrived golden and aromatic, topped with tauhu pok , fucuk , bean sprouts, cucumber, chicken, sambal and a halved lime.
11 things to do at GMBB — Bukit Bintang’s creative mall for food, shopping & art workshops
It looked promising, but to my taste, the broth curiously leaned more toward lontong than laksa . The noodles, a mix of yellow mee and vermicelli, were cooked well, though the sambal didn’t add much heat or flavour. Tasty as it was, it didn’t quite capture the essence of Nyonya laksa I’ve come to expect from places like Melaka or Penang, for example.
The next dish, however, redeemed everything. The Nasi Lemak Ayam Pongteh (RM19) was a nice surprise. While the rice itself was a little firm and the sambal veered into sambal berlado territory with its sweetness, sourness, and blended onion-saturated texture, the pongteh itself was magnificent.
The gravy was thick, umami -rich with mushroom and taucu , yet balanced enough to let sweetness and savouriness mingle. The chicken was tender enough to fall off the bone and carried the sauce like a perfect duet. This, without question, was the highlight of my meal.
On a whim, I ordered Pai Tee (RM16) . The shells were crisp, the flavours alright, though the filling leaned on the lighter side. A touch more jicama would have made it feel more generous, but it was a pleasant bite nonetheless.
Curiosity then pulled me towards Omah Jawa, the other half of this culinary marriage. My choice was Rawon Komplit (RM18) , a bowl of beef soup with rice, bean sprouts, and sambal belacan .
The broth was deep, aromatic, and comforting, its spice notes of peppercorn and star anise blooming with every spoonful. The beef, marbled with delicious bits of fat, melted effortlessly in the mouth.
For something fried, I tried the Bakwan Jagung (RM12) , 6 plump fritters meant to be bursting with corn. While crunchy and well-seasoned, they leaned closer to onion fritters than corn-filled ones. Sambal kicap on the side was addictive but drowned out the little corn flavour that remained.
A final note on drinks: don’t leave without trying Baba Tea (RM5) or Nyonya Coffee (RM6) . Both are sweetened with gula melaka , giving them a richness that makes you want a second round.
Final thoughts
Limapulo Terrace is a place where history and hunger meet on equal footing. Come for the architecture and the atmosphere, and you’ll be rewarded with a heritage house that feels alive with stories. Stay for the food, and you’ll find some gems worth savouring — particularly the Ayam Pongteh and Rawon .

Which Korean food spot in KL is worth the drive?
summary: Limapulo Terrace in Bukit Bintang pairs Peranakan dining with Javanese cuisine at Tong Shin Terrace, a preserved 1930s heritage building. Diners can explore its historic interiors, rent kebayas and sample dishes such as Nyonya Laksa, Ayam Pongteh and Omah Jawa’s Rawon, with mains from RM18. It is particularly suited to those seeking traditional flavours alongside a heritage dining experience.
title: Limapulo Terrace: Michelin Guide-listed Nyonya laksa, nasi lemak ayam pongteh & Nusantara delights in a 1930s Peranakan building

body:
A hidden, cosy gem along the bustling East Coast Road , DJDH Ramen Restaurant immediately stands out with its warm neon lighting and colourful storefront. Stepping inside, you’re greeted by its friendly host, Sandra, whose warm demeanour instantly makes you feel like a longtime friend.
The decor is equally striking, pairing that same neon glow with a vast collection of anime figures that transports you straight to the heart of Tokyo.
Unlike a typical Tokyo establishment, however, DJDH Ramen Restaurant serves up unique fusion ramen broths — think laksa and herbal bak kut teh -inspired broth paired with springy noodles. They also offer affordable student meals, making it a perfect spot for students from the numerous nearby primary and secondary schools.
What to order at DJDH Ramen Restaurant
I opted for the Signature Herbal Ramen (S$22) and the Tomato Wagyu Essence Ramen (S$29) . Both dishes are also included in their student meal promotion, which lets students enjoy a bowl of ramen and a drink for just S$10 .
Each set lets you choose between pork, beef, or vegetarian options; I went with beef for the herbal ramen and pork for the tomato ramen. Do note that the Tomato Wagyu Essence Ramen is a weekly special and may not always be available.
First, I dug into the Signature Herbal Ramen (S$22) , which arrived in a cooking pot seemingly fresh off the stove. Inside was a generous bed of noodles adorned with strips of beef and herbs, garnished with a pinch of seaweed strips.
The warm, mellow flavour of the herbal soup was instantly comforting and felt really wholesome and restorative, like something your grandmother would boil up for you. The soup had a smooth, bright profile with a subtle sweetness likely from red dates and goji berries, which are used in Chinese soups to lend a honey-like lift to round out the astringent herbs. It was also deeply aromatic, carrying a well-rounded, earthy fragrance.
Overall, it was well-balanced, light, and non-greasy. I enjoyed the broth so much that I drank every last drop!
The noodles were cooked to a spot-on al dente, offering just enough resistance for a pleasant, toothsome bite. While slightly thinner than conventional thick, yellow ramen noodles, they still made for a thoroughly satisfying slurp.
The beef was thinly sliced shabu-shabu style, guaranteeing a tender bite thanks to its quick cooking time. Each strip was clean and savoury without feeling tough or sinewy, offering a firm yet tender chew that complemented the texture of the noodles well.
We tried Singapore’s highest-rated ramen
Next, I got started on the Tomato Wagyu Essence Ramen (S$29) . The steaming pot sports a vibrant orangey-red broth, containing thin strips of pork and cabbage, finished with some seaweed strips.
It struck a stark contrast to the first ramen. While that bowl was more mellow in flavour, this tomato broth was bright and invigorating, with the tomato giving the soup nice tart and tangy notes.
I was pleasantly surprised that the wagyu flavour did come through in the broth. Its slightly rich, beefy undertones complemented the tangy tomato well and added body and dimension to the broth. Meanwhile, the sliced cabbage lent a subtle sweetness which balanced the bowl out perfectly.
The noodles were prepared as well as they had been in the first dish, and were nicely al dente with a good bite. The slightly thicker tomato soup also clung on to the noodles slightly more for a more flavourful mouthful. The pork was also cut shabu-shabu- style in thin, tender strips that didn’t lean too fatty or greasy.
I recommend pairing the ramen with their house-made chilli oil, crafted with beef tallow, if you like a numbing, spicy kick to your meal.
For meat lovers, DJDH Ramen Restaurant also offers luxurious cuts of Japanese A5 Wagyu Steak (starting from S$79 for 100g) garnished with punchy pink peppercorns and various pickled sides and seasonings. If steak isn’t your thing, try out the Signature Double Chicken Chop (S$22) , which is glazed in their proprietary sauce for a delicious, glistening finish and served with earthy shimeji mushrooms.
Who is DJDH Ramen Restaurant best for?
DJDH Ramen Restaurant is best for diners who enjoy unique Asian fusion creations and Japanese cuisine, as well as those who appreciate warm, hospitable service. They even offer tabletop games to play while waiting for your meal — perfect for keeping the young (and the young-at-heart) entertained.
With its generous student discounts, it is an ideal, budget-friendly spot for youths. Its vibrant, anime -themed interior also makes it a great fit for anime enthusiasts and anyone looking to snap Instagram-worthy shots.
How to get to DJDH Ramen Restaurant
DJDH Ramen Restaurant is located along East Coast Road and a quick 8-minute walk from Marine Terrace MRT Station (TEL27) . The station connects to the Thomson-East Coast MRT line. Use Exit 3 and walk towards Telok Kurau Road before turning left onto East Coast Road.
…
summary: DJDH Ramen Restaurant on East Coast Road pairs an anime-themed interior with Asian-fusion ramen broths, including herbal bak kut teh and laksa-inspired creations. Mains range from S$22 to S$79, alongside S$10 ramen-and-drink sets for students, located an 8-minute walk from Marine Terrace MRT. The restaurant is best suited for students on a budget, anime enthusiasts, and diners seeking casual fusion meals with tabletop games.
title: DJDH Ramen Restaurant: Affordable student meals & cosy fusion ramen on East Coast Road

Chocolate and curry: the collaboration nobody saw coming. Did you know why people add chocolate to curry? It’s actually for depth, not sweetness. Monster Curry and Meiji have cooked up a Christmas Menu , and we’re here to intrigue you! Stay open-minded now; don’t knock it till you’ve tried it.
Curry-mas
Credit: Monster Curry x Meiji
The star of the collaboration is the Meiji Black Choco Katsu Curry (S$16.90) , with Meiji Black Chocolate melted into Monster Curry’s demi-glace curry sauce. This combination is surprisingly a common go-to secret ingredient used by the Japanese as well, adding a richer hue to the sauce.
Credit: Monster Curry x Meiji
For a playful touch, try the Meiji Black Choco Curry Fries (S$8.90) ; either dip or drizzle the chocolate-infused curry onto the fries.
Choco-mas
Credit: Monster Curry x Meiji
This festive season, it’s the perfect time to bring your kids to Monster Curry! Why, you might ask. Simple: the Monster Curry and Meiji Christmas collaboration is made for them. Sweeten the season with the Chocolate Noel Honey Toast (S$14.50) . Think buttery and chocolatey, with fresh strawberries, toasted marshmallows, and Meiji’s Chocorooms.
Credit: Monster Curry x Meiji
A favourite among children is the Choco or Strawberry Cone Milkshake (S$6.90) , bringing together a festive indulgence.
Merry Workshop
Credit: Monster Curry x Meiji
Another reason to bring the little ones to Monster Curry is the Meiji Holiday Toast Workshop (S$32.90) , eligible for 1 adult and 1 child . This workshop set includes the Toast Set and decorative ingredients, a Snack Platter consisting of Tori Karaage and Fries, Homemade Iced Lemon Tea and Ribena, and a Goodie Bag with S$25 worth of Monster Curry Vouchers and Meiji merchandise , including a Meiji Tumbler and more!
The workshops are held over the weekends at these selected 4 Monster Curry outlets :
• Northpoint City (28 to 29 November)
• Jurong Point (5 to 6 December)
• Suntec City (12 to 13 December)
• VivoCity (19 to 20 December)
Do note that sessions are limited to 2 per day , from 2pm to 3.30pm and 3.30pm to 5pm , with a limit of 16 pax per session !
Your Loyalty, Rewarded
It’s time to experience how well curry and chocolate go together! Earn and redeem rewards through Monster Curry’s Gifts of Christmas stamp card promotion, with 1 stamp for every S$25 spent on a single receipt, and a bonus stamp when you order the Chocolate Noel Honey Toast or Meiji Black Choco Katsu Curry .
Credit: Monster Curry x Meiji
The more you eat, the more you earn. Collect 3 stamps to unlock a free Deck-The-Toast DIY , 6 stamps for a free Katsu Curry Rice (pork or chicken ), and 9 stamps for a free Meiji Black Choco Curry . Reach 12 stamps and a S$25 Monster Curry voucher is yours.

ARMYs, December is shaping up to be a BTS month. With BTS making their highly anticipated return to Singapore for 4 sold-out concerts on 17th, 19th, 20th, and 22nd December , their fans have plenty more to look forward to than just seeing their favourite septet on stage.
In fact, Singapore is getting the full BTS treatment with BTS THE CITY ARIRANG , a month-long celebration featuring everything from dazzling light shows and exclusive merchandise pop-ups to themed parties and photo spots.
So, whether you’ve already secured your concert tickets or simply want to soak up the BTS vibe, here are 21 BTS-themed activities in Singapore to check out this December.

12th-22nd December 2026
Image for illustrative purposes only.

You might have watched the Supertrees light up to Christmas tunes before, but this December, Gardens by the Bay is giving its iconic light show a BTS twist.
As part of BTS THE CITY ARIRANG, the Supertrees will come alive with a special 15-minute light-and-music showcase featuring BTS hits. Expect colourful illuminations synchronised to the group’s music, transforming one of Singapore’s most recognisable landmarks into an experience for ARMYs.
That’s not all. The Supertrees will also be illuminated in Ari Red from 11pm to 1am , so fans can snap some photos even after the main show has ended.
If you’re hoping to catch the spectacle without spending a cent, head to the designated viewing points around World of Plants, including Secret Life of Trees, World of Palms, and Fruits and Flowers. Otherwise, you’ll need a Christmas Wonderland ticket to watch from within Supertree Grove.

body:
Beauty in The Pot launches new all-you-can-eat hotpot buffet
Image credit: Lu Angels via Google Maps
Just in time for the holiday season, Beauty in The Pot (BITP) is launching its first-ever buffet hotpot concept on 25 November 2026 , available exclusively at The Star Vista . In addition to its signature hotpot menu, you can expect a spread of cooked dishes, including dim sum, Japanese katsu curry rice, laksa and more.
The buffet also features an extensive dessert section, with freshly made waffles, tofu gelato, cakes, soft serve, DIY chendol, and even a chocolate fountain. There are three buffet tiers to choose from: Standard Buffet (from $23.90++ per person) , Deluxe Beef and Seafood Buffet (from $32.90++ per person) , and Luxury Wagyu and Seafood Buffet (from $45.90++ per person) . All three have a 90-minute dining limit, with prices varying by dining period and day of the week.
If you’re not a fan of hotpot, good news: you can still try out the new cooked food menu at the Weekday Hi-Tea Buffet ($15.90++) , available Monday to Friday from 2:31pm to 4:30pm.
We were lucky enough to try the Luxury Wagyu and Seafood Buffet, and here’s what we thought of the new launch.
24 Best Hotpot Restaurants In Singapore, Including Steamboat Buffets
Food at Beauty in The Pot Buffet
We started with the new Japanese katsu curry rice, and I was pleasantly surprised by the quality of the dish. The curry had a punchy flavour, with a good balance of sweetness and spice. We didn’t get to try the pork katsu, but the chicken katsu tasted like standard chicken tenders.
Next, we got the laksa, which was pretty decent too. The soup was creamy and aromatic, while the noodles were thick and bouncy.
What sets the laksa apart is the DIY factor, allowing you to customise your bowl with extra taugeh, chilli paste, fish cakes and more.
Of course, we had to sample a little of everything from the hot food lineup: yakitori , char siew buns , chicken sausages , chilli crab buns and many more.
Overall, everything was tasty and of good quality, but my personal favourite was the char siew bun, which was fluffy with a generous sweet -savoury meat filling.
The yakitori was also tender and well-marinated.
We moved on to BITP’s specialty: their hotpot. We selected our soup base from four classic bases: Tomato with Sweet Corn Soup Base, Authentic Pork Bone Soup Base, Spicy Soup Base , and Cordyceps Flower with Mushroom Soup Base , and four signature bases available with an upgrade (from $5++) : Beauty Collagen Soup Base, Herbal Drunken Chicken Soup Base, Cooling Coconut Soup Base , and Rich Prawn Soup Base .
We opted for a quart pot and tried the Pork Bone, Spicy, Beauty Collagen, and Rich Prawn Soup Bases. The prawn base stood out for being exceptionally rich, with a briny, sweet, and umami seafood flavour.
Image credit: Beauty in The Pot
For proteins, the Japanese Beef Wagyu Chuck Eye Roll was richly marbled and incredibly tender. We also got the US Pork Belly , which was much fattier than what I was used to. It had an indulgent, melt-in-your-mouth texture, perfect for those who enjoy rich, fatty cuts of meat.
Lastly, the dessert section had an impressive selection of goodies. The Belgian waffles , egg waffles , and souffle pancakes were all worth trying, especially since the chef makes them fresh right in front of you. You can also drizzle them with your favourite sauces, such as Biscoff or chocolate, to make them extra indulgent.
The snow ice station was another favourite of mine, as you can build your own ice kacang or chendol with your choice of toppings.
Another unique dessert was the Tofu Gelato, which had the familiar taste of soya beancurd but with the smooth, creamy texture of gelato.
13 Best 1-For-1 Buffet Deals In 2026, From $28++ Per Person
Ambience at Beauty in The Pot Buffet
Beauty In The Pot’s Star Vista outlet was cosy and comfortable, with well-maintained interiors and cushioned seating. The slightly upscale ambience makes it a suitable spot for catching up with friends or celebrating special occasions.
The restaurant is located on the second floor of The Star Vista, just a five-minute walk from Buona Vista MRT Station , making it easily accessible.
Beauty in The Pot Buffet–Eatbook Review
Overall, given the quality and variety of food on offer, the new hotpot buffet offers great value for money. The hotpot lives up to the high standards BITP is known for, while the selection of cooked dishes adds variety to the meal. If you’re a big eater, I’d definitely recommend giving this buffet a try.
With the holiday season right around the corner, check out IKEA’s Christmas buffet back for just $29.90. And if you can’t get enough of hotpot, here are some of the best hotpot buffets in Singapore you can visit.

Hot Burg is a new hamburg steak restaurant in Buona Vista
Image credit: Hot Burg
One-north office folks and Buona Vista regulars, your lunch rotation just got a meatier option: Hot Burg is a new hamburg steak restaurant at The Star Vista .
Japanese Hamburg Chain Opens First SG Outlet In CBD—Here’s Our Review
Every set comes with at least two 100% Wagyu hamburg steaks , along with unlimited rice, soup, and grilled veg. The best part? Sets start at $18.80++ if you’re a member.
Image credit: Hot Burg
Opened on 26 October 2026 , this homegrown spot is the brainchild of 29-year-old co-founder Ambrose Mak, who ate at more than 40 hamburg restaurants across Japan, China, and Malaysia before working out his own beef blend and seasoning.
Image credit: Hot Burg
The beef is ground fresh and shaped by hand, and it’s only grilled once you order. Each patty is served on your own tabletop hotplate. It arrives at medium, so you can leave it to sizzle a little longer if you like yours more done.
Image credit: Hot Burg
There are two sets to pick from: the 2 pcs Wagyu Hamburg Set ($23.80++, or $18.80++ for members) and the 3 pcs Wagyu Hamburg Set ($26.80++, or $21.80++ for members) . Your first patty is always the Original, which comes seasoned. After that, you can have another Original at no extra cost or switch to a different flavour.
Image credit: Hot Burg
The Cheese Burger (+$3 per piece) is basically a DIY cheeseburger kit. It comes with two brioche buns, house burger sauce, caramelised onions, and sharp cheddar, and staff shaves Grana Padano over the patty at your table. You can stack it into a proper burger or just eat it straight off the plate.
For something lighter on the palate, the Roasted Tomato Burrata (+$2/pc) tops the beef with roasted tomato and a creamy round of burrata.
Image credit: Hot Burg
Every set comes with free-flow Chef’s Golden Chicken Broth, grilled broccoli and potatoes, and Niigata rice, which is a pretty generous spread for the price. If two or three patties still don’t fill you up, you can add extra ones a la carte. These range from $10.80++ for an Original ($8.80++ for members) to $18.80++ for the foie gras version ($13.80++ for members).
To finish, there are six house condiments to play with: House Yakiniku, Yuzu Ponzu, a smoky chilli blend called Gunpowder, Chilli Oil, Salt & Pepper, and House Pickles.
The restaurant has 40 seats and sits on the second floor of the mall, a short walk from Buona Vista MRT Station .
In other hamburg news, Japanese chain Yamamoto’s Hamburg recently opened its first SG outlet at Lau Pa Sat. We liked its juicy beef hamburg, and it also does a Singapore-exclusive chicken patty. If you’d rather have your beef in a bun, check out our ranked guide to the best burgers in Singapore .
Address: 1 Vista Exchange Green, #02-17, The Star Vista, Singapore 138617
Opening hours: Mon to Sat 11am to 9pm, Sun 10:30am to 8:30pm
Tel: 8825 7360
Website
Hot Burg is not halal-certified.

body:
Take A Bre is a waffle kiosk in Chinatown
Image credit: Peiching Tan
Growing up, one of my favourite desserts has always been old-school waffles —the kind you get from under-HDB bakeries. I love them for how warm and satisfying they are, not to mention the variety of flavours to choose from. It seems like this beloved treat is here to stay, and some have put their own twist on it, from mochi to nian gao filling. We recently found Take A Bre , a kiosk right outside Chinatown Complex that has gone viral for its crispy waffles in an extensive range of flavours.
10 Best Old-School Waffles Ranked, Filled With Biscoff Spread, Sea Salt Caramel And More
Image credit: Take A Bre via Google Maps
This humble waffle stall is run by 35-year-old Yu Shu Fen, who used to work as a pastry chef for well-known bakeries and cafes, including the likes of Dimbulah Coffee. With her education in Pastry & Baking at ITE College West and years of experience in the industry, she was well on her way to becoming a sous pastry chef.
However, things took a turn when she became the main caregiver of her elderly mother after her father passed away from a stroke back in 2023. Needing more time and flexibility, she quit her job and decided to start Take A Bre in 2025, selling waffles and Hong Kong-style egglets.
Image credit: T greensake via Google Maps
The shift was not easy at first, having to juggle low footfall and the many expenses of running a F&B business. Slowly, the shop started gaining traction online for both Shu Fen’s perseverance and, of course, her delicious waffles.
With more exposure, Take A Bre is now known as an up-and-coming waffle store, offering more than 20 flavours to choose from.
Image credit: Brandon Lim
Unlike most heartland bakeries, their waffles boast a crispier exterior and soft centre, and are served with generous filling. It’s definitely thicker and more hearty than the old-school waffles we’re used to. Shu Fen also makes her own batter from scratch, with a recipe she developed after much trial and error.
Image credit: John Tan via Google Maps
Their best-selling flavour would be Nutella ($3.50) , followed by the Biscoff ($4) and Banana Nutella ($4.50) . Another contender would be the Kaya & Butter ($3.50) , where the waffle is slathered in copious amounts of kaya and served with thicc slabs of butter.
Image credit: X L via Google Maps
The kunafa trend has made its way here too, with the Pistachio Kunafa going for $5 . For a more decadent and sinful treat, they also have Ice Cream ($6) waffles that come with two scoops of ice cream to beat the heat.
Image credit: Denise L via Google Maps
If sweets ain’t your thing, their savoury options look just as enticing, with lesser-seen flavours such as Truffle ($5) and Chicken Floss & Mayo ($5) . Purists can opt for their Plain/Kosong waffle ($2.50) , which is also the cheapest item on the menu.
They’ve recently expanded their menu, ranging from classic Red Bean & Butter ($3.50) to bolder flavours such as Garlic Butter Cheese ($4) , Salted Egg & Chicken Floss ($5.50) and even Spicy Konjac ($3) .
Egglets are also up for grabs. Prices start from $10 , and each one comes topped with a scoop of ice cream.
Each waffle is made-to-order, so do expect a wait and head down earlier before taking a bre-ak to try these waffles for yourself.
Take A Bre is a three-minute walk away from Chinatown MRT Station .
For more interesting bakes, our Sweet Stuff coverage features a homegrown bakery serving coriander chiffon cake. In other news, World Christmas Market 2026 is making a return to Fort Canning with free entry from next month.
Address: Unit 11 Trengganu Street, Singapore 059029
Opening hours: Daily 12:30pm to 8pm
Website
Take A Bre is not halal-certified.

Feature image adapted from Take A Bre and X L via Google Maps.
summary: Run by a former pastry chef, Take A Bre is a waffle kiosk in Chinatown serving waffles from $2.50 with over 20 variations to choose from!
title: Get Loaded Waffles From $2.50 At This Viral Chinatown Kiosk, Run By An Ex-Pastry Chef

body:
When it comes to the comfort food I’m obsessed with, hor fun will always be somewhere close to the top of my list. I enjoy it in all its glorious forms — the traditional san lou (sliced fish and beansprouts), seafood, or savoury beef hor fun. Just offer me a plate and I’ll happily make room for it, even if I’ve just eaten. This time, I’ll be taking my hor fun obsession to Alexandra Village Food Centre , where I’ll be putting 2 stalls — Ding Sheng 鼎升 and Hor Fun Premium — to the test to see which one truly does this dish justice.
What is beef hor fun ?
A Cantonese classic, beef hor fun is a fragrant and delicious local zi char dish. Flat rice noodles are wok-fried over high heat for a few moments, then tossed with beef slices, dark soy sauce, spring onions and green veggies, and bathed in a starchy, silky egg gravy.
What makes a good beef hor fun ?
Since I’ve been eating hor fun all my life, I’d like to think of myself as somewhat of a connoisseur. A good rendition should have tender, flavourful beef, tossed with smoky, wok hei -rich sheets of hor fun that are slightly chewy and have a satisfying bite. The silky egg gravy should have sufficient body to coat the ingredients without being overly thick, while delivering a well-balanced savoury flavour that won’t leave you overwhelmed.
Why these contenders?
Having been around since 2015, Hor Fun Premium has been serving customers at Alexandra Village Food Centre for more than 10 years. In 2024, the stall relocated to the centre row within the same premises. When Ding Sheng 鼎升 took over its former unit in that same year, several people were left confused, thinking they were seeing double. With 2 establishments serving much the same zi char fare under one roof, it was only natural that I pit them against each other.
Ding Sheng 鼎升
The newer of the two, Ding Sheng 鼎升 , is manned by 4 uncles in their 50s and 60s, and service is prompt and efficient. The bulk of the menu comprises hor fun , rice, and mui fan dishes, as well as a droolsome photo of a bowl of Prawn Paste Chicken (S$12 for 8 pieces) that nearly made me succumb to temptation. However, I had one mission and wasn’t about to let anything distract me: the Beef Hor Fun (S$6) .
The sheets of hor fun were completely drenched in the golden-brownish-hued thick egg gravy, complemented by a substantial amount of beef slices, green vegetables, and served with a side of pork lard bits.
I started by slurping on the gravy. It was a tad more savoury than usual, giving me the impression that the chefs might have gone a little overboard with the seasoning. However, the flavour mellowed with each subsequent mouthful, especially when paired with the flat rice noodles. Speaking of which, they had the perfect texture, with a slight chew and a robust wok smokiness.
The beef slices were incredibly tender while still tasting like, well, actual beef! I’m glad the stall didn’t go trigger-happy with the meat tenderiser, which can sometimes leave the beef with an unnaturally soft texture and an almost artificial bite. I noticed this while working on one of my recent beef hor fun features.
Fried pork lard on a plate of beef hor fun ? Now, that’s something I don’t see every day! When the uncle asked if I’d like some, I didn’t need a second ask. And boy, was I glad I said yes! The crispy, fatty morsels added another layer of shiokness to the dish, and I’m now secretly hoping this becomes the new norm.
Poh Preserved Veg Hor Fun: Shangri-La ex-chef sells smoky wok-flavoured chai poh hor fun in Chinatown
Hor Fun Premium
Given that Hor Fun Premium has been around for quite some time, I had my expectations cranked up notch. Much like Ding Sheng, the stall had a whole brigade of senior chefs working in the small kitchen. They appear to be slightly older in age and more weathered.
Right off the bat, I could tell that the gravy of Hor Fun Premium’s Beef Hor Fun (S$6) had a more substantial amount of egg — they were in large clumps! Visually, the entire dish looked almost identical to the one I ordered from Ding Sheng 鼎升. Serving it in a bowl was a smart move, as I could dig into the hor fun without having to worry about spilling the sauce all over the table.
The chefs had nailed the texture of the hor fun , matching its competitor bite for bite. However, while there was some wok hei , it wasn’t quite as punchy as the one from Ding Sheng. The beef was executed well, too — soft, tasty and smooth. I was satisfied.
Remember how I mentioned that Ding Sheng 鼎升’s gravy tasted overly savoury at first but grew on me? The gravy at Hor Fun Premium was less salty, though it started to taste a little bland after a few mouthfuls.
Verdict
Ding Sheng 鼎升
Hor Fun Premium
Price
S$6
Portion
On par
Flavour
Strong wok hei with flavourful gravy
Slightly less wok hei , with gravy that could be more flavourful
Ingredient Quality
Very good
…
summary: Alexandra Village Food Centre is home to two competing zi char stalls, Ding Sheng 鼎升 and Hor Fun Premium, both offering Beef Hor Fun at S$6. Compared on their wok hei, gravy, beef tenderness and portion sizes, Ding Sheng edges ahead with smokier noodles and more flavourful gravy, making it the stronger choice for diners craving a savoury plate of beef hor fun.
title: Alexandra Village beef hor fun Showdown: Ding Sheng 鼎升 vs Hor Fun Premium

Are you already making a list and checking it twice? ‘Cos we sure are! It’s the time for festive shopping and we’re looking to Tangs The Christmas Store 2026 for a variety of gift-ready picks all in one place. Beyond that, we’re also eyeing seasonal finds that are perfect for getting our homes in the festive mood. If you need a place to start, here are a few finds worth adding to your shopping list.

For the person who deserves a little pampering
Photography: Tangs
Ever wanted to skip the usual candles and get one with a carousel on top? Well, now you can with Diptyque’s carousel topper ($150), which you can pop on top of any of its classic candles. Make your own gift bundle by pairing it with a Diptyque candle of choice to surprise your giftee with something that smells good and doubles as decor.
Speaking of aromatherapy gift bundles, there’s also a ready-made one by Moss St. Ceramics. The Hamptons Collection mini soy candle and diffuser gift set ($89, U.P. $129) comes in blue and white floral ceramic vessels, with a gift box to match.
For beauty treats, highlights include SK-II’s Pitera best collection ($143) that’s dressed up in festive packaging; La Mer’s The Lifting Hydration Collection ($1150, worth $1435); the Penhaligon’s Halfeti Gift Set ($255); and M.A.C.’s signature satin lipstick set ($133, worth $210).
For the host who’s bringing everyone together
Photography: Tangs
When you’re attending a festive house party, it’s only courteous to bring something for the host who whipped up the feast. Pleasingly, Tangs The Christmas Store has you covered with its dining and kitchen essentials.
Snag the Smeg Glossy breakfast set in red ($428, U.P. $536) for a kitchen counter statement; a three-piece sake set from Wanokokoro ($38, U.P. $58) for a minimal but elevated drinking vessel; or the festive Christmas tree-shaped bowls from Now Designs by Danica ($36 for a set of six, U.P. $45).
For the Christmas table
Photography: Tangs
Pitching in on the office spread, or turning up to family dinner with dessert in hand? Keep a couple of edible gifts in your back pocket. Tangs The Christmas Store has everything from festive nibbles like the Holiday Village butter cookie set from Beryl’s ($18), to full-on platters like the cheese and charcuterie gift box from The Dempsey Project ($106.90).
On the hunt for panettone? Bag this seasonal treat from Bonifanti by Culina – get the panettone classico glassato ($48.50 for 750g) for a traditional glazed version, or the panettone farcito al pistacchio ($65.50 for 750g), for an indulgent take that’s filled with pistachio cream and finished with chocolate.
For decking the halls this Yuletide season
Photography: Tangs
If your favourite part of Christmas is getting the decorations out, save some time for the Christmas Shop. You’ll find glass baubles ($15.20 each) and paper star hanging ornaments (from $10.40) – useful if your tree could do with a few new additions.
Starting with the tree itself? The mix-leaf Christmas trees with lights come in 6ft, 7ft and 7.5ft sizes (from $399.20, U.P. from $499) There are smaller decorations too, including Elephant Parade’s Christmas ornaments ($48).
Ready to shop?
The Christmas Shop is at Tangs at Tang Plaza Level 3 until 27 December and Tangs at VivoCity Level 2 until 28 December. You can also shop the Christmas selection on Tangs.com until 18 December.
For another festive shopping stop, the Christmas Market runs at VivoCity’s Level 1 Atrium from 1 to 27 December, and at Lot One’s Level 1 Atrium from 7 to 27 December. Here’s a sneak peek of what to expect: there’s gift ideas like a Sanrio characters gift box from Sugarsmith ($85); a box of premium floral teas from Tea Therapy Singapore ($24.90 for eight pieces); Craftholic plushies (from $12.90); and a Christmas Club cookies gift set from August Signature ($46.80, U.P. $78).

There are few things in this world that pair as perfectly as wine and cheese. And since we can’t say no to a glass of vino now and then at our favourite wine bar , you can bet we’re always on the hunt for the best gourmet cheese in Singapore.
From creamy brie to nutty gruyere and bold blue cheeses, these cheese shops in Singapore stock everything you need to build the perfect cheese board . Whether you’re planning a picnic , hosting a dinner party or simply craving a good wedge of fromage, these spots deliver the goods. Let’s get cheesy, y’all!
Why trust this guide
Every shop on this list offers something new and caters to every taste. Our team has meticulously gone through reviews and information about cheese shops across Singapore to curate the most diverse and helpful combination. All these listings are up to date and accurate on all counts, including price and operational hours.
Where can you buy cheese in Singapore?
The best all-round cheese shop in Singapore is The Cheese Shop in Joo Chiat, an award-winning speciality store stocking artisanal wheels from the UK, France, Italy, Spain and Holland. For rare European finds with a guided pick, go to The Cheese Ark on Stirling Road; and for a family-run deli with vegetarian and plant-based options, The Cheese Deli on East Coast Road.
1. M&T Bistro
Photography: M&T Bistro
A handcrafted farm to table experience offering premium French mountain cheese and other foreign delights, M & T Bistro is the new stop for fromage fanatics! With a focus on the artistry of cheese making, this spot presents a formidable catalog of cheeses for every taste.
Best for: Farm fresh mountain cheese with authentically French items on the menu
Prices: $20 to 30 per pax
Opening hours: Monday to Friday, 11.30am to 3pm and 4pm to 8pm
Address: #01-12, Guoco Tower, 5 Wallich Street, Singapore 078883
Visit M&T Bistro
2. The Cheese Shop
Photography: The Cheese Shop via Facebook
With a name like that, did you really expect anything less than pure cheese heaven? Situated in a beautifully conserved shophouse in Joo Chiat, The Cheese Shop is a speciality store offering an award-winning selection of artisanal goodies from the UK, France, Italy, Spain and Holland. Great for anyone dying to impress guests at your next dinner party with a stellar cheese plate. You can even snag yourself a bottle of wine and dips to make it a feast.
Best for: Award-winning artisanal cheese with wine and dips to host impressive events
Prices: Cheeses at $6.90+; gift boxes and cheese platters at $128+
Opening hours: Varies depending on location
Address: Multiple locations including Joo Chiat and River Valley
Visit The Cheese Shop
3. Cheeselads
Photography: Cheeselads
We love the folks at Cheeselads for the beautiful cheese platters available for small or big groups. But if you’d like to give it a whirl and set your own cheese board up to test your creativity, you can snag gourmet cheeses from this brand too! We’ve got our eyes on some interesting wheels like the green pesto gouda, Sublime Sheep and Glorious Goat.
Best for: Cheese platters for different groups sizes or a dine-in cheese bar experience
Prices: Dine-in at $20 to $30 per pax; cheeses at $10+; platters at $48+
Opening hours: Monday, 4.30pm to 10.30pm; Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday, 12pm to 10.30pm; Friday and Saturday, 12pm to 12am
Address: 117 Tyrwhitt Road, Singapore 207546
Visit Cheeselads
4. Delicia
Photography: Delicia
If gourmet goods strike your fancy, this cheese delivery service in Singapore will spoil you silly. Touting luxurious ingredients like foie gras, oysters, truffle oil and, of course, its own selection of cheeses. Which is basically everything you’ll need to put together a cheese board for a party. Start with cold cuts like Iberico or parma ham, then get your sweet element with jams. Finally, sort through cheeses like manchego, organic feta and smoked scarmorza.
Best for: Creating curated cheeseboards with various ingredients
Prices: Cheeses at $10+; cold cuts at $13+
Opening hours: Wednesday to Friday, 2pm to 7pm; Saturday and Sunday, 12pm to 6pm
Address: #02/09, 251A Arcadia Road, Singapore 289847
Visit Delicia
5. GourmetShop
Photography: GourmetShop
The brainchild of chef Julien Bompard from the now-shuttered Le Saint Julien restaurant, GourmetShop offers the finest French and European cheeses. Like our personal favourite, the signature creamy truffle brie. Or if you’d rather leave it to the experts, the store also offers ready-made cheese platters – perfect for parties and get-togethers.
Best for: Professionally crafted charcuterie platters and fine French cheeses alongside ready-to-eat gourmet meals
Prices: Ready meals and cheeses at $49+
Address: Available online
Visit GourmetShop

Photography: Chelsea Pridham via Unsplash

Outram Park Ya Hua Rou Gu Cha is leaving PSA Tanjong Pagar Complex. The Teochew bak kut teh shop at 7 Keppel Road serves its last bowls there on Thursday 31 December 2026, then reopens further along the same road, at Tanjong Pagar Distripark, in January 2027.
Last day at Keppel Road is 31 December 2026; the new shop opens in January 2027. Detail from Ya Hua’s moving notice. Image: Outram Park Ya Hua Rou Gu Cha
The shop broke the news to customers on Facebook on 20 November, with a moving notice that sets out both addresses. It is a relocation, not a closure. The yellow signboard and the round tables at Keppel Road have a little over five weeks left.
Where Ya Hua is going
The new shop is at Block 37 Keppel Road, #01-02A, Tanjong Pagar Distripark, Singapore 089064, in the same complex as the Singapore Art Museum . Ya Hua’s notice names Cantonment as the nearest MRT station; it is one of the three Circle Line stations that opened on 12 July . Both shops sit on Keppel Road, close enough for regulars to walk from the old address to the new one.
The month is fixed but the day is not. Ya Hua has given January 2027 for the reopening, with no date and no opening hours for the new unit yet.
Ya Hua’s moving notice: from 7 Keppel Road to Block 37 Keppel Road, #01-02A, Tanjong Pagar Distripark. Image: Outram Park Ya Hua Rou Gu Cha
The last weeks at Keppel Road
Until 31 December the old shop keeps its usual hours: 7am to 11pm from Tuesday to Saturday, 7am to 10pm on Sunday, closed on Monday. That early start is the reason Keppel Road works as a breakfast stop as much as a supper one. Ya Hua has not published separate hours for Christmas Day, which falls on a Friday.
What a bowl costs
The house style is Teochew: a clear soup led by pepper and garlic, with the pork ribs as the main event. These are the prices listed on Ya Hua’s website for the main soups and sides; they may change, particularly after the move:
• Spare ribs soup: S$8
• Pork ribs soup: S$7
• Sliced pork loin soup: S$7
• Pig’s stomach soup: S$8
• Fresh sliced fish soup: S$8, S$10 or S$15
• Braised pig’s trotters: S$7 or S$10
• Braised fried beancurd: S$3 or S$5
• Fried dough stick: S$2
Tea is charged by the table rather than the cup. The website lists S$4 for one or two people, S$5 for three or four, and S$6 for five or more, with Tie Guan Yin and 913 King’s Tea among the leaves.
Under the Ya Hua signboard in 2009, from the restaurant’s own photo gallery. Image: Outram Ya Hua Bak Kut Teh
The Havelock Road outlet
Ya Hua’s second outlet, at 593 Havelock Road, #01-01/02, Isetan Office Building, is not part of the move. It opens from 11am to 10pm, Tuesday to Sunday, and closes on Monday, so it is a lunch and dinner shop rather than a breakfast one. Bak kut teh before work stays a Keppel Road habit, at the old address until 31 December and at Distripark from January.
Outram Park Ya Hua Rou Gu Cha details
Current address: 7 Keppel Road, #01-05/07, PSA Tanjong Pagar Complex, Singapore 089053
Hours until 31 December: Tuesday to Saturday 7am to 11pm, Sunday 7am to 10pm, closed Monday
Last day at Keppel Road: Thursday 31 December 2026
New address: Block 37 Keppel Road, #01-02A, Tanjong Pagar Distripark, Singapore 089064
Reopening: January 2027, exact date not yet set
Nearest MRT for the new shop: Cantonment (Circle Line)
Phone: 6222 9610
Website: yahua.com.sg
summary: Outram Park Ya Hua Rou Gu Cha serves its last day at PSA Tanjong Pagar Complex on 31 December 2026 and reopens at Block 37 Keppel Road, Tanjong Pagar Distripark, in January 2027.
title: Outram Park Ya Hua Rou Gu Cha leaves Keppel Road on 31 December and reopens at Tanjong Pagar Distripark in January

What’s better than Korean food? Affordable Korean food, of course! You might be familiar with Sagye, but did you know that it actually has a sister concept named Sagye Lite , which sells its beloved Sotbap (pot rice) for a much more affordable pricing?
Credit – Sagye Lite @ VivoCity
Grab your friend(s) as Sagye Lite is opening its 2nd outlet in VivoCity on 25 Nov 202 6, with an opening promotion available. It will be running a special 1-for-1 Sotbap promotion for 6 days, from 25 to 30 Nov 2026 . Diners who purchase an eligible Sotbap will receive a second one of equal or lower value for free — hooray. Do note that the promotion applies to all of the available Sotbaps on the menu except for the Signature Beef Short Rib (S$34.80) and F1 Japanese Wagyu Striploin (S$52).
Credit – Sagye Lite @ VivoCity
The promotion is available across 2 daily redemption sessions : lunch from 11am – 3pm and dinner from 5pm – 10pm. Do note that it is capped at 150 redemptions for each session daily . Get ready to head down early if you want to snag this 1-for-1 deal. Additionally, no advance reservations are allowed; you must place your order and dine in person to secure your redemption.
Credit – Sagye Lite @ VivoCity
There are plenty of Sotbaps for you to choose from for this 1-for-1 deal with various different meats. If you love pork, get the Grilled Pork Belly (S$13.90) or, to spice it up a little, opt for the Stir-Fried Kimchi with Pork Belly (S$12.90) . Chicken lovers, choose between Grilled Chicken (S$12.90) , Spicy Chicken (S$12.90) or Spicy Chicken with 3 Cheese (S$18.90) .
Credit – Sagye Lite @ VivoCity
Truffle lovers are sure to enjoy Truffle Egg White Seafood with Mushroom (S$18.90) . There are also Smoked Duck (S$16.90) and Collagen Ginseng Chicken (S$20.90) options . Other choices include Beef Bulgogi (S$18.90) , Mapo Tofu (S$12.90) , and Grilled Eggplants with 3 kinds of Mushroom (S$12.90) .
You’ll be able to tuck into their sides such as Kimchi Pancake (S$12.90) and Rose Tteokbokki (S$18.90) to complement your meal too. Don’t miss out on this good deal, and I hope you manage to be one of the first 150 people to redeem this deal!

Diners can choose from affordable Korean pot rice dishes priced from S$12.90, with exclusions for two premium beef options. The deal is available for dine-in only during lunch and dinner sessions, with 150 redemptions per session daily, making it useful for diners seeking a budget-friendly Korean meal who can visit early.

How to plan a funeral in Singapore
Trigger warning: This article talks about death. There is also a brief mention of murder and suicide in the “What to do immediately after the death occurs” section.
Death is a natural part of the life cycle, but that doesn’t mean it’s an easy subject to navigate. Losing a loved one can be difficult. Adding on the responsibilities of planning a funeral may be even more overwhelming.
Here’s where we come in. From reporting the death and planning a funeral based on religion, down to distributing assets of the deceased, this is a step-by-step guide for planning a funeral in Singapore .
What to do immediately after the death occurs
In the hospital
It’s not uncommon for patients to pass away while they’re receiving treatment at a hospital. If the patient is hooked up to an EKG machine, a flatline is enough to alert medical personnel to check on their condition. If they aren’t, alert a nurse or doctor to attend to the patient immediately.
Image credit: Homage
The on-call doctor will then certify the death, which includes noting the cause of death for the death certificate. The next-of-kin (NOK) will then be able to download a digital copy of the death certificate on the government website, LifeSG .
At home
Deaths that occur at home follow a similar procedure, except that a doctor needs to come to the home to verify the death. You may contact the deceased’s most recent attending doctor for this. If they are not available, any other doctor who’s able to make a house call will do.
Image credit: Pexels
Once the cause of death has been verified, the NOK will be able to obtain the digital death certificate of the deceased on My Legacy@LifeSG .
You may also call the police if there is no doctor available. Do note that the police will transport the deceased’s body to Mortuary@HSA in this case. The NOK and other family members will be contacted to come down to identify and claim the body for the funeral.
Overseas
Singapore citizens and permanent residents must have their deaths registered with the ICA Registry of Births and Deaths , even if they passed away overseas. The responsibility lies with the NOK, who’ll need to obtain a death certificate from the country where the deceased died. You’ll then have to report the overseas death on ICA .
You may contact the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for help in this matter. Their consular officers can also help to arrange for undertakers for repatriation of the deceased’s body.
Repatriating the body back to Singapore for burial or cremation is easiest handled by a funeral director here or the undertaker overseas. They’ll be able to help with transport of the casket, as well as the preparation of the following documents required:
• Foreign death certificate
• Embalming certificate
• Sealing certificate
• Coffin export permit from the country where the deceased’s body is
• Airway bill
• Letter of authorisation from the National Environment Agency (NEA) to handle the casket
These documents are to be submitted to the funeral director for the application for the coffin import permit. A copy of the above will need to accompany the casket as well on the flight to Singapore.
To facilitate the importation of the casket, you should inform MFA of the date of arrival and flight number of the plane transporting the casket.
Unknown or unnatural cause of death
In the event that the cause of death cannot be determined, the case is then handed over to the police. The police will then transport the body to the Mortuary@HSA, located within Singapore General Hospital.
Image adapted from: Singapore Police Force
The NOK will be notified as to when they’ll be able to go down to the mortuary to identify the deceased’s body. This is done with a coroner who might suggest an autopsy, should the cause of death not be identifiable.
If the autopsy confirms that the death is unnatural, such as suspected murder or suicide, there will be a need for further investigations by the police. The family will only be able to collect the deceased’s body and digital death certificate once an investigating officer contacts them.
Preparing for a wake & funeral service
After death registration comes preparations for the wake and/or funeral. You and your family should decide on the type of wake and/or funeral service for the deceased. This could be based on their religious beliefs or what the family would prefer.
Once that’s settled, you can engage a funeral director to help with setting up the wake and funeral, as well as cremation or burial procedures. My Legacy has a directory of funeral directors categorised by religion.
How much does a funeral cost in Singapore?
A funeral costs about $1,000 for a direct cremation or burial package. A 3-day wake package usually starts from $3,000 . There are also fees to be paid to NEA, which is usually around $100 for cremation, $500-$900 for a niche at a columbarium, or $315-$940 for a burial.

With festive parties and sumptuous feasts filling our calendars, let’s face it: hardly anyone is in the mood for boring deadlines and projects in December. But before you continue to begrudgingly trudge through these torturous weeks till the 25th, we found something to add a little sparkle to your work days. Bring on these Christmas 2026 food deals and self-care treats in the CBD!
Perfect for anyone working in the CBD (or just visiting the area), these festive deals conveniently located at One Raffles Place will make it feel like Christmas came early. Grab your work crew and head down to the mall from now till 30 December 2026 to enjoy these $15 dining deals and $50 self-care treats. Ready for some holiday magic?
Christmas 2026 food deals in the CBD
1. Fun Toast
There’s nothing like a warm cup of kopi or tea, and classic toast to bring some comfort to the work day. Fun Toast is one of our go-to local spots at One Raffles Place, and it’s celebrating the festivities with a special Yuletide treat: the X’mas salted egg chicken and ham French toast for a divine sweet-savoury combination. Enjoy this Christmas spin on French toast, along with chicken rendang rice and a beverage at $15 (U.P. $19.10).
Address: Fun Toast , #B1-02, One Raffles Place, 1 Raffles Place, Singapore 048616
2. Drips Bakery Cafe
Photography: Drips Bakery Cafe
When the mid-day cravings for a sweet treat hits, make your way to Drips Bakery Cafe for picture-perfect pastries. This artisanal bakery is known for buttery tarts in an array of fruity and nutty flavours, as well as indulgent cakes. Specially for the holiday season, enjoy a slice of the signature Black Forest cake and a slice of the eggless honey lemon cheesecake at $15 (U.P. $25).
Address: Drips Bakery Cafe , #01-08, One Raffles Place, 1 Raffles Place, Singapore 048616
3. Grains & Co.
Photography: Grains & Co.
Is eating good and feeling good your go-to mantra? Grains & Co. lets you do so even during the holiday season with wholesome and delicious grain bowls. Tuck into a nutrient-packed bowl of grains, proteins, greens and homemade dressings, with the option to personalise your creation. Up for some sweet savings? Get the Jingle bowl, a bowl of seasonal soup and a Fruity tea for just $15 (U.P. $18.70).
Address: Grains & Co. , #B1-10, One Raffles Place, 1 Raffles Place, Singapore 048616
4. Namino Hana
Photography: Namino Hana
If your usual salad bowls are feeling like rinse-and-repeat, switch things up with a Japanese bento box from Namino Hana. Take your pick from deliciously marinated proteins like chicken teriyaki, deep-fried salmon teriyaki, and grilled pork belly with sea salt and garlic seasoning, and enjoy them over a bed of Japanese premium rice. Psst: the limited-time festive deal lets you enjoy a unagi bento, a mixed salad and a cup of green tea for only $15 (U.P. $20.50).
Address: Namino Hana , #B1-23, One Raffles Place, 1 Raffles Place, Singapore 048616
Christmas 2026 self-care treats in the CBD
5. Hanguk Skin Solutions
Skip the flight to South Korea, and easily get your K-beauty fix at Hanguk Skin Solutions. This Korean beauty salon uses only machines and skincare products from Korea, and offers the full works of facial, body and hair treatments. The salon also prides themselves on transparent pricing and zero hard-selling, so you can unwind in peace. If you’ve been coveting soft, radiant and smooth skin, here’s your sign to enjoy two Crystal Ice Brazilian hair removal sessions at $50 (U.P. $760)!
Address: Hanguk Skin Solutions , #02-25/26, One Raffles Place, 1 Raffles Place, Singapore 048616
6. Amber Beila
As the year winds down, it’s the perfect excuse to indulge in some well-deserved self-pampering. For a luxurious beauty experience without the hefty price tag, head to Amber Beila. Facial, body and hair removal treatments, they do them all. Plus, every treatment will be personalised to your specific skin type, needs and wants. Want a deep-cleanse to revitalise your skin? Treat yourself to a customised facial with extraction at $50 (U.P. $298).
Address: Amber Beila , #05-19A, One Raffles Place, 1 Raffles Place, Singapore 048616
More jolly deals and treats at One Raffles Place
Photography: Perky Lash
And that’s not all! More dining deals await, including Cha Re Re (#B1-19) – enjoy a bento bowl, a stew and a beverage at $15, U.P. $21.90 – and Randy Indulgence Acai Bar (#B1-39) – enjoy a large acai bowl and a fruity stick at $15, U.P. $20.90.
Plus, get a dental consultation and a 3D scan at Nuffield Dental (#05-19) at $50 (U.P. $162), or pamper your peepers with a collagen lash lift with tint and eyebrow shaping session for $50 (U.P. $76) at Perky Lash (#04-21).
With a dazzling array of festive food and self-care deals, there’s no reason not to treat yourself this Christmas season – especially if you’re hustling near the CBD. Don’t work near the CBD? No fret, One Raffles Place is mere steps away from Raffles Place MRT Station, so it’s easily accessible.

Hong Jiu Claypot is a new Sichuan restaurant in Jurong East
Image credit: Angie Ang via Google Maps
Chinese eateries have taken Singapore by storm lately, introducing us to a wide range of cultures and cuisines, from Yunnan cuisine to traditional Fujian delicacies . Amongst the new wave of restaurants lies Hong Jiu Claypot . Located in Jurong East , they’re all about bold Sichuan flavours.
30 Best Chinese Restaurants In Singapore, Including Private Rooms And Michelin-Starred Options
Image credit: Hong Jiu Claypot
Hong Jiu Claypot is run by a husband-and-wife duo, passionate about serving authentic and high-quality food that embodies Sichuanese cuisine. Leading the kitchen is Chef Wang Yunchang, a Sichuan culinary veteran. With over four decades of experience and having won two national gold awards, it’s safe to say that the food here is in good hands.
Image credit: DAniel Tan via Google Maps
Though our little red dot is no stranger to this cuisine, what makes them stand out is the thought that goes into each dish. Take, for example, their signature 9-Minute Prawn Vermicelli Claypot (price TBD) , where the prawns are handpicked, and the onions are layered to prevent burning.
Alluding to its name, this dish is cooked tableside for exactly nine minutes. Diners get to witness the cooking process up close and personal, right in front of them.
Image credit: Hong Jiu Claypot
Other claypot dishes sound just as yummy as they look, including the Slow-Braised Beef Brisket (price TBD) and Golden Broth Sliced Beef (price TBD) . The former features meaty beef brisket chunks doused in a thick gravy and served with potatoes, while the latter is paired with a lighter, clear broth. Folks who prefer chicken can go for the Braised Chicken (price TBD) claypot instead, which looks equally spicy and flavourful.
Image credit: Hong Jiu Claypot
Their vegetable and side claypots are not one to miss, featuring classics such as Tomato Scrambled Eggs (price TBD) and Hand-Torn Cabbage (price TBD) . The standout here has got to be the Crab Roe Silky Tofu (price TBD) for a more decadent and umami treat.
Image credit: Hong Jiu Claypot
Seafood lovers will be in for a treat, as they also have grilled whole fish. If you can handle spice, the Mala Grilled Fish (price TBD) would definitely bring the heat.Otherwise, the Garlic Grilled Fish (price TBD) is another contender.
The restaurant is currently holding exclusive opening promos. Get the Mix & Match Claypot Set ($24.90++) that comes with your choice of one fish, one meat, and one vegetable or claypot dish. On top of that, you can enjoy the Signature Fragrant Spicy Crab ($9.90++) with a purchase of the Mix & Match set.
If you’re dining solo, one-person sets are also available from just $10.80++ , comprising one main dish, a cold dish, and free-flow rice and drinks.
That’s not all—diners who spend $29.90++ on a single receipt can enjoy a glass of free beer, as well as a $10 cash voucher that can be redeemed instantly.
Do note that the promos are available for a limited time only. As the restaurant has been gaining traction lately, it’s best to call ahead to ensure you get a table and enjoy the promotions while you can.
The cherry on top is the eatery’s location, which is a short five-minute walk from Jurong East MRT Station .

body:
Project Smoked is a popular smokehouse in Taman Sentosa JB
Whenever my friends and I crave barbecue in Johor Bahru , we almost always end up at a K-BBQ joint. It gets repetitive, though, so we were looking for ways to spice things up. When I heard about Project Smoked , a smokehouse with legit American BBQ, I decided to head down and see if it could earn a spot as my next go-to spot.
The current exchange rate is RM1 = ~SS$0.31 as of 24 November 2026.
Food at Project Smoked
The difference between Korean and American barbecue comes down to cooking technique. K-BBQ typically involves cuts such as samgyeopsal and galbi, cooked over high heat through direct table-side grilling and often cut into bite-sized pieces.
American barbecue, on the other hand, centres on larger cuts such as brisket, ribs, and sausages, slow-cooked over indirect heat and wood smoke for hours until the tough connective tissue breaks down, resulting in genuinely tender meat.
The founder shared that while studying in America, he worked at a local barbecue joint, where he learned the art of Texas-style barbecue. When he returned to Malaysia, he wanted to bring the same concept home, and so Project Smoked was born.
Project Smoked prides itself on trimming and dry-rubbing each cut of meat by hand every day, and smoking using only Malaysian mangrove wood, which imparts a cleaner, more subtle smokiness than other types of wood.
To try their barbecued meats, we ordered their signature Black Angus Short Rib (RM108++ for 160g) and Honey Iberico Burnt Ends (RM45++ for 150g) , which came with fluffy dinner rolls, pickles, and three sauces—barbecue sauce, yuzu habanero sauce, and spicy chilli sauce. Each sauce had a distinct flavour profile: the barbecue sauce was slightly sweet yet smoky, while the yuzu habanero was bright, tangy, and spicy. Meanwhile, the spicy chilli sauce reminded me of chicken rice chilli, with punchy flavours of garlic and ginger.
My favourite dish of the whole meal was the Black Angus Short Rib. It was smoked low and slow for up to 16 hours, resulting in fall-off-the-bone tender meat perfumed with a smoky aroma. It was also finished with a sprinkle of flaky salt, which brought out the meat’s natural sweetness. Though I liked it on its own, I found that the barbecue sauce gave the dish some extra oomph.
The Honey Iberico Burnt Ends were also a close runner-up, featuring chunks of pork belly dry-rubbed and smoked for six hours. This reminded me of a zhnged-up version of char siew: it was melt-in-your-mouth tender, with a rich, buttery mouthfeel. The fat was so beautifully rendered that the meat and fat practically melded together, making each bite indulgent without being overly fatty.
I enjoyed this most when paired with the chilli sauce. Its punchy, piquant flavours complemented the rich, slightly sweet pork, creating a well-balanced bite. My dining companion, however, preferred it with the yuzu habanero sauce, as its tartness helped cut through the richness.
The staff also recommended the Typhoon Smoked Tongue (RM38++) , comprising beef tongue smoked for six hours and generously topped with a blend of chilli crisp and panko.
As someone who hasn’t tried beef tongue before, I was initially skeptical. However, it quickly became one of our favourites: the meat was soft and succulent, with a deep, beefy flavour, while the panko added a sweet-spicy element that enhanced the dish and provided some textural contrast.
We also had some of their sides to round out our meal. We got the fan-favourite Loaded Cheese Thots (RM30++) , featuring a bowl of tater tots tossed in a barbecue-flavoured seasoning blend and loaded with pulled pork. It’s then topped with a flame-torched blend of cheeses and drizzled with sriracha mayo.
My dining companion fell in love with this dish almost instantly, and it’s no surprise why. The tater tots were addictively crispy on the outside with a fluffy interior, which contrasted nicely with the soft, smoky pulled pork. The sriracha mayo was creamy and tangy, brightening the whole dish while adding a little kick, and the smoky, charred flavour of the cheese tied everything together.
Their Southern Mac & Cheese (RM20++) was another standout, featuring al dente elbow macaroni tossed in a creamy sauce that’s made with four cheeses: gouda, mozzarella, parmesan, and cheddar. The whole shebang is then topped with a sprinkle of herb-seasoned panko.
This was honestly one of the best versions of mac and cheese I’ve had. It was really creamy and cheesy, pairing nicely with the charred meats. I liked that they used gouda and cheddar, which gave the dish a more luscious mouthfeel, while the parmesan added a savoury depth to keep things from tasting one-note.
Ambience at Project Smoked
…
summary: We visited Project Smoked, a smokehouse near Mid Valley Southkey dishing out legit American BBQ, to see if it's worth the hype.

MODU opens in City Hall with 12 Korean samgyetang flavours
If you’ve given up on MODU because of the queues at Mandarin Gallery , here’s another chance to get a bowl. MODU recently opened its third Singapore outlet at Raffles City on 18 November 2026 .
Image credit: MODU
This one serves the full line-up of 12 samgyetang flavours, and two of them aren’t sold at any other outlets in Singapore.
12 New Korean Eateries That Opened In 2026: DIY Bibimbap, Fresh Shio Pan And More
MODU first made a name for itself at Mandarin Gallery , where it was dubbed Singapore’s first samgyetang specialty restaurant . It then opened a larger, 12-flavour outlet in the CBD, which we covered in our MODU High coverage .
Image credit: MODU
The Raffles City outlet has the same hanok-inspired look as the others, with walnut timber, paper-lit panels, and warm, low lighting. It’s a good-looking spot for a long family dinner, but it also works for a quick weekday lunch.
The broth is the main draw. MODU says it uses cage-free chicken raised without hormones or antibiotics, and puts in twice the usual amount of chicken. The broth simmers for 12 hours, then the chicken cooks in it with the herbs for another two hours. Every bowl also comes with free-flow herbal soup refills, so you won’t run out of broth before you finish the chicken.
Image credit: MODU
Let’s start with the two Raffles City exclusives. The Mugwort Samgyetang ($37++) uses ssuk, the Korean mugwort that’s in season every spring. It gives the soup a green, earthy smell and a lighter, cleaner taste than the herbal classics.
Image credit: MODU
The Curry Laksa Samgyetang ($40++) is the one Singaporeans will probably be most curious about. It’s the whole chicken in a rich coconut-based laksa broth instead of the usual clear soup. MODU says this is the first time it has been offered in Singapore. If you’d rather have noodles, there’s also a Curry Laksa Kalguksu (price TBD) .
If you prefer the classics, the Classic Herbal Samgyetang ($35++) is the cheapest bowl and the easiest place to start. Other options include the Spicy Herbal Samgyetang ($37++) with bean sprouts and radish, the Beauty Collagen Samgyetang ($37++) , the creamy Perilla Seed Samgyetang ($38++) , the Black Garlic Samgyetang ($42++) , and the Black Chicken Samgyetang ($42++), made with silkie chicken.
Image credit: MODU
Coming in a group? There are also sharing plates, such as Grilled Eel served with two house-made sauces, Butter Grilled Abalone , and Fried Fresh Ginseng with honey. Prices for the sharing plates are TBD .
View this post on Instagram
To celebrate the opening, MODU is running a promo for diners who bring their parents. For every two samgyetang you order, you’ll get one Grilled Eel for free. Just show the campaign post on MODU’s Instagram page, @modu.singapore, to the staff when you order. The promo runs until 18 December 2026 .
For more food to try around the area, check out our Raffles City food guide . If you’re after Korean food that’s easier on the wallet, read our guide to cheap Korean food places in Singapore .
